# Talagaja: a documented palm-seed food

**Tala khaja is Ahimanikya’s name for the later seed-food stage shown in his photograph, distinct from ice apple.** The best-supported botanical comparison is the edible spongy **haustorium** inside a germinating palmyra seed. Matching that exact photographed specimen and the khaja/gaja names remains an inference, not a specimen examination.

## What changes inside the seed?

A seed-development experiment explains how the haustorium expands into the space occupied by the endosperm, drawing on stored reserves and supplying the developing seedling. It is a temporary structure; “final food stage” describes the user’s culinary sequence, not the end of the plant’s life. [Ragul and colleagues, 2022, p.503](https://nopr.niscpr.res.in/bitstream/123456789/60086/1/IJEB%2060%20%2807%29%20498-509.pdf).

| Stage or part | Keep the food identities distinct |
| --- | --- |
| Young-fruit endosperm | Earlier food stage associated here with ice apple |
| Ripe fruit pulp | Ingredient used with rice flour for tala pitha |
| Germinated-seed interior | Spongy haustorium; best-supported comparison for the pictured late-stage food |
| Developing underground seedling | A different organ from the spongy interior; do not transfer sprout/tuber recipes automatically |

The anatomical study used seeds from Tamil Nadu. It explains development, not Odisha harvest dates or local names.

## Odisha evidence and eating traditions

Panda and colleagues document **Talagaja** as the edible interior of germinated mature palm seeds. Their account places germination in **October–November** and describes a sweet, crunchy food extracted from the seed covering. The fieldwork ran from April 2015 to March 2018 in selected areas of ten named Odisha districts, involving 93 interviewees. This is historical selected-area evidence, not a statewide calendar or food census. [Original Odisha study, p.67](https://reference-global.com/download/article/10.2478/arls-2021-0031.pdf).

A separate horticultural food paper calls the spongy material **Thavan** and describes fresh/raw consumption. It also documents drying and milling experimental flour. That process is research evidence, not a tested Odisha household recipe or shelf-life guarantee. [Food-processing study](https://annexpublishers.co/full-text/JNH/6103/Physico-Chemical-and-Functional-Characteristics-of-Palmyrah-Borassus-flabellifer-L-Spongy-Haustorium-Flour.php).

## Local names need their own evidence

A 2019 Kantio Katha vocabulary post links several regional words to palm-seed sprout or interior. These descriptions do not yet identify exactly the same edible tissue. They are saved as attributed language leads, not verified aliases. [Original Odia post](https://kantiokatha.blogspot.com/2019/07/blog-post_23.html). The user’s tala khaja wording is preserved; the primary Odisha study’s Talagaja spelling is preserved separately.

## Food, science and possible enterprise

A useful editorial story is **one palm, several foods across its life stages**. Fresh seasonal food and experimental flour offer two distinct research directions. Laboratory composition of dried powder cannot be used as a nutrition label for the fresh food in the photograph. Current Odisha prices, traded quantities, producer margins, product-specific exports and validated shelf life remain unknown after this bounded search. No commercial success or health benefit is inferred.

The supplied photograph remains a local research reference with an attachment hash in the food register. Its original creator and public reuse rights have not been verified.

[Related reading](tala-pitha.md) — Explains distinct maturity stages of palm foods; no equivalence to tala khaja is asserted.

# Tentuli: fruit, seed and the collector economy

**Tentuli is tamarind, *Tamarindus indica*.** The pulp used in food, the hard seed, seeded sale lots and de-seeded pulp need separate records.

## Season and food uses

The Balasore field survey conducted in **January 2018–February 2020** records **January–April** fruiting for tentuli. It describes pulp in pickles, chutney and curry, and tender leaves as a vegetable. These are reported uses, not fully specified recipes or present market availability. [Table 1, row 72, printed p.455](https://www.botanyjournals.com/assets/archives/2020/vol5issue3/5-3-106-999.pdf).

SCSTRTI's historical community study lists **Titel / Tentuli** among products marketed in its **Lanjia Saora, Jantar** village account (Table 2.16, printed p.50). This adds community and place attribution without establishing quantities or earnings. Its seasonal tables also mention occasional tamarind-seed gruel, but near-identical tables across communities and missing cooking endpoints make this a lead for local review, not a publishable recipe. The report's fieldwork/publication dates remain unresolved; 2014 occurs in the repository filename. [Study](https://repository.tribal.gov.in/bitstream/123456789/74427/1/SCST_2014_research_0338.pdf).

## Follow the collector's sale

Vasundhara's *MSP Denied* records **Sitarani Hasda of the Rairangpur region** reporting a sale of **two quintals for ₹5,000**. This is a historical self-reported transaction; the interview date and seeded/de-seeded grade are unclear. It is not an Odisha price average, net profit or a current quote. The same booklet includes collectors' accounts of difficulty accessing procurement. [Ground testimonies, PDF p.11](https://vasundharaodisha.org/upload/pdfFile/b949225825e4667de86b4628a67b57b8.pdf).

The booklet's policy rates and statewide production claims require original dated records. TDCCOL's tender could not be retrieved through the web or direct download; no tender quantity, achieved procurement or realised sale is adopted. This matters for the eventual business story: a support price, collector receipt and finished-product retail price describe different stages.

## Forest origin and cultivation

The Balasore source classifies its entries as wild edible plants; this does not certify the origin of market lots. ICAR-CIAH lists a tamarind cultivar, **Goma Prateek**, showing a separate horticultural research pathway. Odisha planting, named local cultivars and the split between forest, community and privately grown supply remain unverified. [Institutional list, SVRC row 4](https://www.icar-ciah.org/index.php?do=veriti_relese_svrc&mod=veriti).

body:
# Berhampuri Patta

**Let the border catch your eye. Then ask how it became part of the cloth.**

A textile can give you a reason to look at a city differently. Berhampuri Patta opens that possibility for Berhampur in Ganjam: a silk surface, a patterned edge, and the work that joins them. The first encounter can begin with one detail rather than a vocabulary lesson.

## A border and an end panel

The official Odisha weaver directory describes its Berhampur Patta examples as silk in both warp and weft—the two directions of yarn in the fabric. It identifies temple-shaped *kumbha* border designs and an extra-weft end panel called *Salari anchal*. Its table describes plain weave with three-shuttle work and additional weft motifs.[^handloom-weaver-directory]

These are descriptions of documented examples. Choose a border detail and a detail in the decorated end of a saree, then ask someone knowledgeable how each was formed. Seeing the yarn or work on a loom would make that answer more tangible, if a maker agrees to show it.

The examples give us a way to begin looking. They cannot certify the fibre, construction or maker of another cloth offered for sale.

## What does joda name here?

In *Mapping Indian Textiles* (2017), **Ruchira Ghose** identifies the Berhampur sari and joda as textiles, distinguishing the sari for women and joda for men. Her Berhampuri section also names kumbha and phoda motifs.[^handloom-mapping2017]

That distinction matters when researching the tradition. Our earlier source check recorded an Incredible India page describing joda as bridal bangles. We use the attributed textile account here and retain the disagreement in the notes below. A tourism description should not quietly change the identity of the thing being described.

For a piece you encounter, ask its wearer or maker what they call it, how it is used and whether a particular occasion gives it significance. Record the explanation with its source; do not assume that an institutional summary answers every local question.

## Put a production name beside the place

The directory associates its examples with **Berhampur Cotton & Silk Weavers Co-operative Society Ltd.** and **Choudeswari Silk Weavers Co-operative Society Ltd.**, both listed in Berhampur, Ganjam. Their illustrated profiles include sarees, joda, dhoti, chaddar and stoles.[^handloom-weaver-directory]

Those names are documentary starting points. A visit, order or demonstration needs current confirmation from a willing host. The directory is undated, and the information here does not establish that a particular service or product is available today.

If you buy a piece, keep its documented maker or production-group credit, fibre description and care advice with the receipt. A place name draws you towards the tradition; the details of a particular cloth help you remember the work itself.

## Carry the question towards the coast

The earlier story idea paired this textile with a southern-coast feature. Begin that reading path with [Gopalpur](../places/gopalpur.md), or compare the ways of noticing cloth in [Habaspuri](habaspuri.md) and the wider [loom-to-market story](../stories/handlooms-from-loom-to-market.md).

This is an invitation to research a journey, not a timed route or an arranged workshop. Give the textile encounter room of its own. One explained border may stay with you longer than a hurried list of shops.

<details>
<summary>Sources, disagreement and earlier research</summary>

On 10 October 2026, Ghose’s original PDF page67 and the official directory’s pages19–20 were read and visually inspected from saved documents. Directory table rows12–13 on pages3–4 were re-read. No source photograph is reproduced, and no reuse rights are inferred. Practitioner confirmation of terminology and the structure of a particular piece remains open.

The publisher disagreement below is the saved 2 October finding; the tourism page was not retrieved again in this update. Its bangles classification, loom description and royal-origin narrative are not adopted. This is an attributed choice for our reader profile, not a claim that the publisher has corrected its page.

Creative direction: **Ahimanikya Satapathy**. Developed and document-reviewed by the current AI assistant. Earlier research is retained below without rewriting its evidence. No new independent human review, field visit, cooperative relationship, stock confirmation or current GI status is claimed.

### Earlier research checkpoints

## Sourced knowledge

The tourism reference identifies Berhampuri Patta among Odisha’s silk traditions.[^weaving-tourism]

## Story opportunity

Pair a textile portrait with a southern-coast travel feature.

*Editorial proposal; audience response has not been measured.*

## Next research

Record fibre, construction, attribution and care instructions for a particular piece.

## Connections

[Related knowledge](../places/gopalpur.md) · [Research standards](../about/research-method.md)

[^weaving-tourism]: [Handloom](https://odishatourism.gov.in/content/tourism/en/experience/themes/handloom.html)

## Technique and market evidence · 2 October 2026

Department identifies silk saree/joda; the recovered directory now supplies construction evidence below. Berhampur / Ganjam [Boyanika: seventy-year institutional account](https://boyanika.com/boyanika-wear-your-heritage/) · [Important handloom centres](https://handloom.odisha.gov.in/en/handloomtab/important-handloom-centers) · [Odisha department: handloom product range](https://handloom.odisha.gov.in/en/handloomtab/product-range).

Boyanika route: institutional collection mention. This identifies a research route; current stock and fulfilment are unverified. Named cooperatives and construction are documented below; current production availability remains pending.

[Six-tradition market comparison](garments-and-markets.md) connects textile identity with market evidence. Tradition-level revenue and exports remain unknown.

[Related market evidence](garments-and-markets.md) — Textile identity connects with market routes while maker provenance and financial outcomes remain separate evidence questions.

## Construction evidence · 2 October 2026

Silk textile with kumbha/phoda motifs; joda identified as men’s textile, not bangles. The initial loom-evidence gap is narrowed by the recovered directory below. [Mapping Indian Textiles — Ruchira Ghose](https://ignca.gov.in/PDF_data/Report_Mapping_Indian_Textiles.pdf), Ghose PDF p.67. This is a source-attributed technique description, not certification of every marketed piece.

## A source disagreement to retain

[Incredible India](https://www.incredibleindia.gov.in/en/odisha/berhampur-patta-phoda-kumbha-saree-and-joda) calls the joda bridal bangles. Ghose’s textile report (PDF p.67) identifies it as a men’s textile, matching the saved Development Commissioner description. We exclude the bangles classification and leave the tourism page’s loom/origin narrative unverified. This is a recorded publisher disagreement, not an unreported correction.

## Institutional connection · 2 October 2026

The [departmental GI list](https://handlooms.gov.in/assets/img/104GIregisteredHandloomProducts.pdf), headed **as at 1 September 2026**, names Directorate of Textiles & Handloom, Government of Orissa against this textile (PDF p.5, row88). This identifies the listed registration organization; it does not certify current GI renewal, authorized-user status or stock.

## Cooperative production leads

The [undated official Odisha weaver directory](https://handlooms.nic.in/assets/img/Weavers%20Database/Odisha637322660372253324.pdf) associates this textile with Berhampur Cotton & Silk Weavers Co-operative Society Ltd. (Berhampur, Ganjam; p.3, row12); Choudeswari Silk Weavers Co-operative Society Ltd. (Berhampur, Ganjam; p.4, row13). These are documented product associations. Current operations, orders, visiting arrangements and retail-piece makers remain unverified.

## Recovered loom evidence

The official directory describes **three-shuttle work and extra-weft motifs** in rows12–13 (PDF pp.3–4). Its two cooperative profiles (pp.19–20) identify silk in warp and weft, kumbha temple borders and a Salari anchal with supplementary weft. The description covers documented examples and a product range including saree, joda, dhoti, chaddar and stole. It is not a test of every product sold under the name.

</details>

[^handloom-weaver-directory]: [Official Odisha weaver directory](https://handlooms.nic.in/assets/img/Weavers%20Database/Odisha637322660372253324.pdf), undated. Pages3–4, rows12–13; illustrated production profiles, pages19–20. Saved original document re-inspected 10 October 2026; documented examples and associations, not current operations.

[^handloom-mapping2017]: Ruchira Ghose, [Mapping Indian Textiles](https://ignca.gov.in/PDF_data/Report_Mapping_Indian_Textiles.pdf), 2017, PDF p.67, Berhampuri Sari section. Joda classification and motif names only; adjoining sections describe different textile traditions.

The user selected [Boyanika](https://boyanika.com/) as an ongoing reference on 30 September 2026. Keep it in the research and website-reference set, connected to [Made in Odisha](../collections/made-in-odisha.md).

The homepage groups products by use and material, including sarees, dress materials, ready-to-wear, running fabric, stoles/shawls and home décor. Its navigation names traditions such as Sambalpuri Ikat, Bomkai and Nuapatna/Khandua. These are observed website labels, not an exhaustive classification of Odisha’s textiles.[^boyanika]

## How we can use it

- **Textile research:** follow named traditions to our existing entries, then verify technique, geography and maker attribution.
- **Content organisation:** study how material, tradition and everyday use can offer different routes into the same collection.

Preserve rights and attribution for any future imagery. Product listings are not evidence of sales, exports, maker income or statewide production. Prices, rebates and stock require a fresh check when used; none is saved here as an evergreen claim.

# Odisha garments, cloth and markets

A garment is what someone wears; fibre, weaving technique, named tradition and production place describe different aspects of it. Keep these separate so that a Sambalpuri saree, a shirt made from Bandha fabric and factory-produced apparel are not counted as the same product.

Boyanika’s checked navigation offers research leads for **sarees, three-piece dress materials, kurtis, waistcoats, kurtas, shirts, jackets, dupattas/scarves, shawls and stoles**. Running fabric, home textiles and accessories are additional categories. Navigation establishes advertised categories, not stock, garment origin or export shipments.

## Tradition and cultural context

| Existing tradition | Saved place or process evidence | Detail to deepen |
|---|---|---|
| [Sambalpuri Bandha](sambalpuri-bandha.md) | Western Odisha; historical GI record | Tie-dye process, motifs, named makers and garment forms |
| [Bomkai](bomkai.md) | Silk production in Sonepur/Boudh | Distinguish origin village from present production centres |
| [Khandua](khandua.md) | Nuapatna silk and calligraphy textiles | Text, ritual use and attribution of each piece |
| [Kotpad](kotpad.md) | Mirgan weavers and aul-root dye reference | Maker-reviewed community names, dye process and use |
| [Habaspuri](habaspuri.md) | Kalahandi | Technique and current continuity |
| [Berhampuri Patta](berhampuri-patta.md) | Southern Odisha silk tradition | Construction, ceremonial use and maker provenance |
| [Tussar centres](tussar-centres.md) | Several named weaving centres | Fibre, provenance and disambiguated place names |

These rows reuse saved source checks. They are not a fresh verification of each tradition or a claim that each is exported.

## Market evidence

The [export series](../statistics/textile-and-apparel-exports.md) covers textiles, apparel and handicrafts together. The [2019–20 workforce census](../statistics/craft-livelihoods.md) records weavers and allied workers separately. Neither assigns export income to a named weaving tradition.

The OGD segment-wise resource identifies a parliamentary source, but its rows did not render. Its 2024–25 column covers **April–September 2024 only**. Retrieve the original table before comparing categories. Seek verified Odisha factory production, shipment origin, destination, HS code, quantity, value and year; company-wide garment output cannot be relabelled as Odisha output.

[Structured product and evidence register](../references/data/creative-economy.json).

[Textile export evidence](../statistics/textile-and-apparel-exports.md) — Read garment traditions beside broad sector exports without assigning the aggregate to any named weave.

## From technique to market · 2 October 2026

The same garment form can carry different fibres and weaving traditions. Three Boyanika specimens give concrete examples: cotton Sambalpuri yarn tie-dye, cotton Bomkai threadwork and silk Khandua with temple borders. These seller specifications describe particular pieces; they do not identify individual makers or certify every textile bearing the tradition name.

| Tradition | Production context | Seller evidence | What remains open |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Sambalpuri](sambalpuri-bandha.md) | Bargarh, Barpali, Sonepur | Cotton SKU 6967/A/BO/78 | Named maker and provenance |
| [Bomkai](bomkai.md) | Sonepur and Boudh production | Cotton SKU 6981/A/BO/76 | Piece attribution and dated origin history |
| [Khandua](khandua.md) | Nuapatna / Cuttack | Silk SKU 7928/A/BO/113 | Maker and ritual distinctions |
| [Kotpad](kotpad.md) | Koraput | Institutional collection mention | Named maker and current specimen |
| [Habaspuri](habaspuri.md) | Kalahandi | Homepage tradition mention | Named maker and product route |
| [Berhampuri Patta](berhampuri-patta.md) | Berhampur / Ganjam | Institutional collection mention | Construction and current specimen |

The [structured evidence](../references/data/handloom-markets.json) links each row to original source locations and preserves unknown stock, income and exports. The last three rows are discovery routes, with no verified item availability.

### A sales series still to recover

Original department and survey PDFs could not be fetched in this run. Survey table leads distinguish outlet, exhibition, online and yarn/cocoon sales; these require their complete headings before calculation. Boyanika’s anniversary account also supplies a turnover claim without a financial year. It is held outside growth calculations. No new annual sales series, export total or weaver-income claim is established here. Retry original PDFs on 9 October; meanwhile deepen missing techniques and maker records.

## Reading the loom, crediting the maker

The comparison now distinguishes **Bomkai** supplementary threads, **Habaspuri** border/pallu structures and **Khandua** tying and dyeing before weaving. Ghose’s August 2017 report provides the Habaspuri and Berhampuri context; the Ministry’s product sheets provide Bomkai and Khandua construction. These are attributed descriptions, with overlapping official text treated as one evidence family where appropriate.

The [structured maker credits](../references/data/handloom-markets.json) add Surendra Meher (Barpali, 1991), Chakrapani Patra (Bomkai, 1986), Sarat Kumar Patra (Nuapatna, 1993) and Gobardhan Panika (Kotpad, 2004) from the state award register. They connect people to documented weaving centres; they do not identify the maker of a Boyanika specimen. Panika also appears in the 2018 Padma Shri announcement.

The tourism page’s classification of Berhampur joda as bangles is excluded: textile sources identify a men’s textile. Exact Berhampuri loom operation, current makers/cooperatives, Habaspuri revival chronology and dye botany remain research gaps. No financial PDF retry was made in this batch; the 9 October retry stays in place.

[People and creations](../people/people-and-creations.md) — Named award records connect weaving traditions with credited people, without turning recognition into present workshop availability.

## From a tradition name to a documented organization

The official weaver directory now supplies five cooperative-product associations: Mahalaxmi for Bomkai, Nuapatna No.1 for Khandua, two Berhampur societies for Patta and Chichaiguda for Habaspuri. The department’s GI list, headed 1 September 2026, adds registration-organization pointers for all six traditions. Registration organizations, producers and retail sellers are distinct roles.

Three illustrated creation profiles link Swarnalata Meher, Debaki Meher and Sarat Kumar Patra to particular works. Their reported making durations are scoped examples, with different activities and unknown labour inputs; no wage, productivity or typical delivery-time calculation follows. See the shared structured record for source pages and qualifiers.

The broader sales comparison remains unfinished. Original financial and Habaspuri-study retries remain 9 October. Current workshop/retail stock and image rights still need separate evidence.

# Habaspuri

**Begin at the border. Then let the end of the saree change what you notice.**

A textile can invite two kinds of attention: the first glance that draws you towards its colour, and the slower look that asks how the pattern became part of the cloth. Habaspuri offers a reason to take that second look—and to place Kalahandi on your map of Odisha’s weaving traditions.

## A pattern with more than one direction

In *Mapping Indian Textiles* (2017), **Ruchira Ghose** describes Habaspuri as a cotton-based textile. Her account identifies temple motifs made with additional warp threads along the border, and additional weft designs in the pallav—the decorated end of the saree. Fish, flowers and kumbha appear among the motifs she records. She describes pit or frame looms fitted with a dobby.[^handloom-mapping2017]

The undated official Odisha weaver directory also describes its listed Habaspuri saree as plain weave with extra-warp and extra-weft designs.[^handloom-weaver-directory]

These descriptions give you something specific to ask about. Choose a border detail and an end-panel detail. If a knowledgeable maker is willing, ask how each was formed and which part of the process they would show first to a beginner. The finished surface can become an introduction to decisions you had not known to look for.

This is a reading invitation, not a way to authenticate a saree from a photograph. A published description of a tradition cannot tell us who made a particular piece or whether a seller has described it accurately.

## Give the place and the maker their own names

The official directory associates Habaspuri saree with **Chichaiguda Weavers Co-operative Society** in Kalahandi. A departmental list headed **as at 1 September 2026** also names that society beside Habaspuri Saree & Fabrics and a registration date of **17 July 2012**.[^handloom-weaver-directory][^handloom-gi-list-2026]

That is an institutional connection worth preserving. It is not a current shop listing, a confirmed workshop invitation or proof of the maker of an individual purchase. The registration date is not being used here as the society’s founding date.

For a cloth you encounter, ask for the maker or production group, fibre description and place of making. If the seller knows only part of that story, keep the answer partial. A name supported by evidence is more useful than a complete-sounding story assembled from assumptions.

## Carry a detail home

You do not need to master textile terminology before enjoying the work. Choose one detail that holds your attention and find out what its maker calls it. Ask before unfolding, handling or photographing the piece. If you buy it, keep its care instructions and attribution with the receipt.

A future visit to a weaving centre would need a willing host, an agreed time and clarity about any demonstration fee. No arrangement is established by this page. The pleasure to plan for is an unhurried encounter with a particular cloth and the person able to explain it.

For a wider reading path, [Woven in Odisha](../stories/woven-odisha.md) sets out the proposed maker-led approach. [From loom to market](../stories/handlooms-from-loom-to-market.md) follows other named textile works and the institutions that help cloth reach its audience. Habaspuri deserves its own introduction within that wider story.

<details>
<summary>Sources, unresolved history and earlier research</summary>

The construction description above was checked on 10 October 2026 against Ghose’s original PDF page 68 and the directory’s page 4, row 14. The GI list’s heading and page 5, row 87 were inspected separately. These are attributed documentary accounts; no independent practitioner review or physical textile inspection has taken place. Directory images are not reproduced and their reuse rights are not assumed.

The earlier **“technique remains unverified”** sentence below records an early 2 October checkpoint. The construction evidence added later that day and rechecked above supersedes that narrow gap. Current workshops and the continuity/revival narrative remain unverified.

The Ugrasen Meher revival lead and the society’s formation chronology remain held. An indexed account suggesting 2013 formation and a departmental entry carrying a 2012 GI date may concern different events; neither is silently turned into a founding date. Original report context and society records are still needed. No new retrieval of that held study or local contact is claimed in this update.

Creative direction: **Ahimanikya Satapathy**. Reader profile and source review: current AI assistant. Earlier text remains in Git revision `67028f14` and is retained below as dated research history. Sources keep their original authorship. No newly claimed human approval, maker relationship, stock availability or legal certification.

## Connections

## Construction evidence · 2 October 2026

Extra-warp temple motifs along border; extra-weft pallu motifs; pit/frame loom with dobby. [Mapping Indian Textiles — Ruchira Ghose](https://ignca.gov.in/PDF_data/Report_Mapping_Indian_Textiles.pdf), Ghose PDF p.68. This is a source-attributed technique description, not certification of every marketed piece.

## Maker and cooperative lead

An [indexed tribal-research passage](https://repository.tribal.gov.in/bitstream/123456789/74023/1/SCST_2020_research_0116.pdf) credits Ugrasen Meher of Chicheiguda with revival and mentions a local cooperative. The full report is unavailable; its date and original fieldwork context were not recovered. These remain leads, without an adopted revival date, current weaver count or operating cooperative claim. Retry after 9 October.

The [departmental GI list](https://handlooms.gov.in/assets/img/104GIregisteredHandloomProducts.pdf), headed **as at 1 September 2026**, names Chichaiguda Weavers Co-operative Society against this textile (PDF p.5, row87). (Chichaiguda, Kalahandi; p.4, row14). These are documented product associations. Current operations, orders, visiting arrangements and retail-piece makers remain unverified.

## Cooperative chronology remains open

The newly recovered departmental GI list names Chichaiguda society against a 17 July 2012 registration. This conflicts with a straightforward reading of the previously held 2013 formation claim. Neither source establishes the society’s actual formation date in the evidence reviewed here. Retain both scopes and seek the original registration and study context.

</details>

# Kotpad textiles

**A colour can lead you back to the hands that made it.**

Begin with a red thread. Follow it into a pattern, then ask what happened before the cloth existed. Kotpad invites that slower journey: from a finished surface to dye preparation, weaving and the names behind the work.

## Follow the colour towards Koraput

*Sustainability in the Handloom Traditions of India*, hosted by the Development Commissioner for Handlooms, associates Kotpad’s weaving with the Mirgan community in Koraput district. Its account names cotton yarn, tussar silk and aul roots among the materials, and describes red, maroon, brown and black in the textile palette.[^kotpad-textiles]

The report traces preparation through washing, drying and dyeing before yarn reaches the loom. That sequence gives colour a history. It also gives a visitor a better question: who prepared and dyed the yarn in this particular piece?

Its description is an introduction to a documented tradition. Fibre, dye ingredients and finishing still belong to the individual cloth; natural-dye language alone cannot establish organic certification or measured environmental benefit.

## A small motif, a particular maker

Dastkari Haat Samiti’s 2017 documentation offers another way in. It identifies crabs, fish, vessels and axes among the woven motifs, naming an axe as *tangi* and a fish as *machari*. The story credits text to **Jaya Jaitly**, photographs to **Chirodeep Chaudhuri**, and artisan work to **Gobardhan Panika and the community**.[^kotpad-motifs]

Open the documented images and choose one figure. What does its shape make you notice? Let its maker’s explanation guide any meaning you attach to it. A familiar-looking object can have a story that your first glance misses.

Panika’s name also appears in the Ministry of Home Affairs announcement dated **25 January 2018**, under Padma Shri, with the field Art-Weaving and state Odisha. That document spells his name **Gobaradhan Panika**. The earlier research below retains the spelling variants and a directory’s conflicting 2017 award year; the ministry announcement supports 2018.[^handloom-padma2018]

A credited work and an award record help us name a weaving life. They do not identify the maker of every Kotpad textile you encounter.

## Give the moving story some time

PSBT’s producer catalogue lists **Biswanath Rath’s** *Kotpad Weaving: The Story of a Race Against Time* as a **2018**, **29-minute** film in **Odia and English**, concerned with the textile tradition and natural dyeing.[^kotpad-film]

Follow the producer’s page for viewing information. This profile draws on its catalogue entry; the complete film has not been reviewed here, and current screening availability remains unconfirmed. A documentary can be a companion to learning about the place before you travel.

## Bring home a detail and its credit

If a maker welcomes a conversation, ask about one motif, the fibre and the way this cloth should be cared for. Keep the maker’s documented name with the piece. For a demonstration or workshop visit, agree the host, time, fee and photography permission in advance.

A good encounter leaves room for an answer you did not expect. Write down what was explained, what you noticed yourself, and what remains a question. That is a more useful souvenir than a story you cannot trace.

Continue with [Koraput’s landscape and everyday enterprise](../places/koraput.md), [Habaspuri’s border and end panel](habaspuri.md), or the wider [loom-to-market story](../stories/handlooms-from-loom-to-market.md).

<details>
<summary>Sources, scope and earlier research</summary>

The original textile report was recovered again on 10 October 2026: PDF page49, printed page36, was read and visually inspected, and its hash matches the saved 1 October capture. Motif names and original credits were checked in Dastkari Haat’s source documentation. PSBT’s catalogue metadata and the ministry announcement’s extracted text were checked separately. The ministry PDF screenshot was unavailable, and direct retrieval returned an HTML page; no fresh visual inspection of that award row is claimed.

Community terminology and the interpretation of particular motifs need practitioner review. The report’s botanical identification, generalized gender roles, processing-duration estimate and environmental-impact language are not independently established or adopted as new claims here. Earlier institutional and market notes remain dated history below; this update makes no new assertion about GI renewal, stock or present operations.

Creative direction: **Ahimanikya Satapathy**. Developed and source-reviewed by the current AI assistant. No new human review, interview or field visit is claimed. Source photographs and film are linked, not reproduced; their credits do not confer reuse rights.

The [Odisha department award register](https://handloom.odisha.gov.in/or/publication/major-achievements/jaataiya-paurasakaara-paraapata) lists **Gobardhan Panika**, associated with Kotpad, Koraput, for 2004. Register spelling Gobardhan Panikar; 2018 MHA list prints Gobaradhan Panika. Spelling variants retained; no current commission availability. The [25 January 2018 MHA announcement](https://knowindia.india.gov.in/assets/doc/PadmaAwards2018.pdf) also lists him for Padma Shri in Art-Weaving, Odisha (PDF p.3, serial58).

This identifies the listed registration organization; it does not certify current GI renewal, authorized-user status or stock.

## Retain the award-year correction

</details>

# Sambalpuri Bandha

## Sourced knowledge

Odisha Review identifies Sambalpuri Bandha as GI application 208, certified in 2012.[^odisha-gis]

## Story opportunity

Present the cloth through a named weaver and the decisions behind its pattern.

*Editorial proposal; audience response has not been measured.*

## Next research

Verify present registry status, technique and maker attribution for each featured piece.

## Connections

[Related knowledge](bargarh.md) · [Research standards](../about/research-method.md)

[^odisha-gis]: [Geographical indications of Odisha](https://magazines.odisha.gov.in/Orissareview/2020/Apr-May/engpdf/GIs.pdf)

## Technique and market evidence · 2 October 2026

Yarn tie-dye (Bandha/ikat); specimen cotton warp and weft. Bargarh, Barpali and Sonepur [Boyanika Sambalpuri specimen 6967/A/BO/78](https://boyanika.com/product/black-dark-red-cotton-handloom-sambalpuri-saree/) · [Important handloom centres](https://handloom.odisha.gov.in/en/handloomtab/important-handloom-centers).

Boyanika route: product specification. SKU 6967/A/BO/78. This identifies a research route; current stock and fulfilment are unverified. Individual maker and piece-level provenance absent.

[Six-tradition market comparison](garments-and-markets.md) connects textile identity with market evidence. Tradition-level revenue and exports remain unknown.

[Related market evidence](garments-and-markets.md) — Textile identity connects with market routes while maker provenance and financial outcomes remain separate evidence questions.

## A named weaving-life research connection

The [Odisha department award register](https://handloom.odisha.gov.in/or/publication/major-achievements/jaataiya-paurasakaara-paraapata) lists **Surendra Meher**, associated with Barpali, Bargarh, for 1991. Place-associated awardee; exact Sambalpuri product attribution requires full central award record.

[Maker credits and unresolved attribution](../references/data/handloom-markets.json).

## Institutional connection · 2 October 2026

The [departmental GI list](https://handlooms.gov.in/assets/img/104GIregisteredHandloomProducts.pdf), headed **as at 1 September 2026**, names Directorate of Textiles & Handloom, Government of Orissa against this textile (PDF p.5, row85). This identifies the listed registration organization; it does not certify current GI renewal, authorized-user status or stock.

## Words woven into cloth

The [official product directory](https://handlooms.nic.in/assets/img/Weavers%20Database/Odisha637322660372253324.pdf) credits **Swarnalata Meher** with a silk-warp/cotton-weft Bapta saree and **Debaki Meher** with a cotton Dasa Phulia example using calligraphy and supplementary threads (PDF pp.10–11). These are named creations, providing a stronger starting point for a feature than anonymous textile pictures. The source reports approximately three months and two-and-a-half months respectively, for different described activities; neither figure is a standard production time. Photograph reuse and interviews remain unarranged.

# Bali and Indonesia: three distinct kinds of connection

Ardika and Bellwood’s Sembiran research identifies early Indian contact with Bali.[^maritime-sembiran] Odisha’s official Bali Jatra account commemorates maritime exchange with Southeast Asia, particularly Bali.[^maritime-culture-2025]

## Link carefully

The first supports an archaeological India–Bali connection; the second establishes a contemporary Odisha commemoration. Neither alone proves that every Indian object in Bali came from modern Odisha. The research graph keeps both links without collapsing them into an exclusive origin claim.

## An epigraphic lead

A scholarly discussion references foreign communities including Kling in Javanese inscriptions. This edition records it as a lead: the underlying transcription, dating and geographic interpretation must be checked. The term must not be automatically equated with modern Odia identity.[^maritime-cane-lead]

## Commercial next step

Obtain Odisha-origin exports to Indonesia by product and year, then identify an actual buyer or producer relationship. National India–Indonesia totals cannot fill a state-level data gap.

[Boita Bandana](../culture/boita-bandana.md) · [Country connection matrix](../trade/connection-matrix.md)

[^maritime-sembiran]: [Sembiran: The beginnings of Indian contact with Bali](https://researchportalplus.anu.edu.au/en/publications/sembiran-the-beginnings-of-indian-contact-with-bali/)

body:
# Buddhist learning in Odisha: Pushpagiri and the monastic landscape

**Pushpagiri is a promising research focus for the ancient learning question.** The [Jajpur exhibition](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/the-buddhist-heritage-of-jajpur-jajpur/NwWh9wDVsCTFtg?hl=en), whose story is credited to Live History India, identifies Langudi with Pushpagiri and connects it to Xuanzang’s account. This is a curated interpretation, not our own reading of an inscription or excavation report.

We already maintain [Ratnagiri](../places/ratnagiri.md), [Lalitgiri](../places/lalitgiri.md) and [Udayagiri](../places/udayagiri-buddhist.md). Keep them as distinct archaeological identities. A modern circuit name does not prove they formed one university.

The primary-source checkpoint below now distinguishes the traveller account, excavated identities and competing Langudi interpretations. No institutional ranking, enrolment or uninterrupted modern university lineage is established.

A broader Buddhist history should distinguish Ashokan inscriptions and the Kalinga-war account, later monastic phases, Buddhist philosophical traditions, objects and manuscripts, and living communities. Links to Southeast Asia require evidence for each person, object or text, rather than an assumed universal influence.

## A landscape of learning, with names preserved in clay

The strongest story combines a traveller’s words with named archaeological evidence. Li Rongxi’s translation of Xuanzang describes the people of Uḍa as devoted to learning and then names Pushpagiri monastery. Separately, the ASI excavation report identifies **Simhaprastha Mahavihara at Udayagiri-2** through seals and sealings. These are different evidence types, connected by region rather than assumed institutional identity.

### What the traveller’s numbers mean

The text describes **more than 100 monasteries and over 10,000 monks across Uḍa**, before introducing Pushpagiri. The numbers belong to the wider historical country. They do not describe Pushpagiri enrolment and are not a modern Odisha census. Miracles described at the stupas remain religious testimony. [Li Rongxi, 1996, Fascicle X, pp.269–270](https://bdkamerica.org/download/1865).

### Keep the sites and institutions distinct

| Place or excavation area | What this checkpoint establishes |
| --- | --- |
| [Udayagiri-1](../places/udayagiri-buddhist.md) | Earlier seal-based identification as Madhavapura Mahavihara, reported by ASI |
| Udayagiri-2 | Simhaprastha Mahavihara; original report includes accession-level seal readings |
| [Langudi](../places/langudi.md) | Proposed Pushpagiri identification with a documented scholarly disagreement |
| [Ratnagiri](../places/ratnagiri.md) and [Lalitgiri](../places/lalitgiri.md) | Distinct sites; no single-university merger inferred from the modern circuit |

[ASI 2007,pp.1,12–17,123,141](https://asi.nic.in/admin/publications/ePublicationReportsDetails/download/47). The inscription readings in the Udayagiri report are credited to **Snigdha Tripathy**, and the excavation/report to **Bimal Bandyopadhyay**. This credits the researchers without claiming a new decipherment.

### Why the Langudi identification stays attributed

The report quotes B.N. Mukherjee’s readings and D.R. Pradhan’s identification arguments. It also records Bandyopadhyay’s reservations after a 1999 visit and calls for further examination. The original Langudi inscription articles and plates have not yet been inspected in this project. The2007 disagreement is a dated scholarly record; it does not prove that no later work exists. Do not promote an Ashokan foundation or a contested inscription date to established fact.

### A dated sequence

| Period | Evidence or research milestone |
| --- | --- |
| Seventh century CE | Xuanzang’s account of Uḍa and Pushpagiri |
| c. eighth–twelfth centuries CE | Udayagiri-2 occupation range interpreted in the excavation report |
| 1958–1961 | Ratnagiri excavation under Debala Mitra, recalled in the report preface |
| 1985–86 to 1988–89 | Four earlier Udayagiri excavation seasons |
| 1997–2000 | Udayagiri-2 excavation campaign |
| 2007 | Publication of the ASI report |

Dating a surviving monastery is different from dating Buddhism’s arrival. The report acknowledges difficulty separating layers within the collapsed building; explanations of patronage and decline remain hypotheses. [ASI,Preface,pp.1,41](https://asi.nic.in/admin/publications/ePublicationReportsDetails/download/47).

[Structured evidence](../references/data/culture-learning.json) retains publication editions, passage locations, lower-bound wording, claim types and unresolved readings. [Related reading](../places/langudi.md) — Separates the proposed Pushpagiri identification from the named Udayagiri monasteries.

body:
# Forest livelihoods: a documented history

**Use dated evidence to explain how collection, household knowledge and trading institutions changed.** A publication date is not the beginning of a tradition.

- **1973:** OFDC's institutional history places kendu nationalisation in this year. Its page also describes later deregulation in named areas. This is a historical anchor, not a statement of today's collection permissions. [OFDC](https://www.odishafdc.com/kenduleaf.php).
- **2001:** Nanda and Sutar's Vasundhara study, hosted by FAO, connects mahua and kendu livelihoods with community forest management and fire. Its cases need local attribution; the title/abstract district mismatch remains unresolved. This does not establish one uniform tribal practice. [Original study](https://www.fao.org/4/ad352t/AD352T06.htm).
- **2018 publication:** Mishra and Pradhan examine household use and marketing channels in a six-village Kendujhar sample. Fieldwork dates and full methods still require the original text. [Study record](https://ideas.repec.org/a/ags/injagm/399613.html).

## Extend the timeline carefully

Research precolonial exchange only where dated documentary or archaeological evidence supports it; then examine colonial forest administration, cooperatives, changes in collector rights, women's enterprise and contemporary processing. Retain oral histories as attributed accounts with consent and provenance; no interviews have been conducted for this entry. Study food preservation, seasonal labour and changing household uses alongside laws and commercial institutions.

[Forest foods](../food/forest-foods.md) · [Markets and livelihoods](../economy/forest-products.md).

## Further historical source

The [SCSTRTI food-knowledge study](../sources/forest-scstrti-foodknowledge.md) offers community-specific descriptions. Its selected sections now inform the honey and siali profiles. Repository filename dates require confirmation; historical accounts are not current interviews or universal practices.

## Leaf craft and agricultural seasons

The [siali profile](../economy/siali-products.md) now links a published 2002 Nayagarh maker case to a 2017 Kandhamal value-chain description. They show why household craft, farming and trade should be researched together. These are separate historical contexts, not a time series or a current livelihood census.

body:
# Jagannath: sacred narratives, inscriptions and the making of Puri

Puri’s story can be read through sacred narratives, royal patronage and the material support of worship. A **1225 inscription records land given to support food offerings**. It is a concrete point where devotion, farming and food meet. It does not date the beginning of Jagannath worship or measure today’s temple economy.

## The sacred narrative

In the Purusottama-ksetra-mahatmya translated by G. V. Tagare, Indradyumna is a king at Avanti. He sends Vidyapati to seek the deity; Vidyapati encounters the Sabara devotee Visvavasu. Visvavasu guides him to Nilamadhava and the narrative anticipates Indradyumna’s installation of wooden divine forms. Vidyapati returns to the king with a garland from the deity. These are episodes in this textual telling, with a cosmological setting, not dated biographical events. [Ch.7, vv.4–6,12–14,48–50,85–99](https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-skanda-purana/d/doc370727.html); [ch.8, vv.1–18](https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-skanda-purana/d/doc370728.html); [ch.9, vv.20–34](https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-skanda-purana/d/doc370729.html).

The text’s forest setting and Sabara participants deserve their own account. They do not by themselves establish the date, route or social process by which worship developed. The district’s [Kantilo Nilamadhab account](https://nayagarh.odisha.gov.in/en/tourism/tourist-places/kantilo-nilamadhab) preserves another place association. Utkal has not established a dated transfer from Kantilo to Puri. Other tellings, including Lalita and the mustard-seed episode, need their own named textual sources before being combined with this version.

## A timeline with evidence labels

| Period | What the evidence supports | What it does not establish |
|---|---|---|
| Sacred narrative time | Nilamadhava, Visvavasu, Vidyapati and Indradyumna in the cited Purana chapters | A CE year for the origin of worship |
| Twelfth century | The saved Odisha government history attributes the present temple to Anantavarman Chodaganga | Sole authorship of every later structure or the first worship at Puri |
| 26 June 1225, Sircar’s conversion of Saka 1147 | Record 1: Suru-senapati’s grant of three vatis of land supports offerings of milk, ghee, rice and curds to Purusottama | Current land ownership, present kitchen quantities or an uninterrupted menu |
| 5 January 1237, Sircar’s conversion of Saka 1158 | Record 2: Khanda, described as a footman, grants land for offerings; the formula places Anangabhima beneath the divine sovereignty of Purusottama | A precisely dated founding ceremony or modern constitutional relationship |
| Saka 1158, records 3–4 | Further grants for offerings; the editor flags calendar discrepancies | Unqualified exact day/month claims for those two records |

The epigraphic anchor is D. C. Sircar’s edition of **four inscriptions in the Patalesvara shrine within the Jagannath complex**. He describes their language as old Odia with some Sanskrit. This is also a route into Odisha’s language history. [Epigraphia Indica XXX, article 34, printed pp.197–200; PDF pp.274–277](https://ignca.gov.in/Asi_data/35546.pdf).

Sircar distinguishes the Madala Panji construction tradition from Ganga family records crediting Chodaganga, and reports the scholarly interpretation that Anangabhima completed work begun by Chodaganga. Record 2 names Halin, Chakrin and Subhadra, while its final sentence remains difficult to interpret. A dated inscription in the complex is not itself a foundation certificate. His suggestion about the Patalesvara shrine’s earlier use is a question, not an established earlier sanctum. [Edition, pp.197,199](https://ignca.gov.in/Asi_data/35546.pdf).

## Follow the connections

The land-and-offering record gives [Mahaprasad](../food/mahaprasad.md) a historical research connection. It supplies no meal count, workforce total or sales figure. The source’s tentative rice-weight conversion and suggested daily frequency remain outside public statistics.

Existing [Raghurajpur](../culture/raghurajpur-pattachitra.md) research connects painting with Jagannath traditions; the repository’s destination account already carries the craft-process and revival material. Reuse that record rather than create another village profile. A link between devotional subjects and makers’ work does not quantify craft income or prove that all production serves pilgrimage.

Connects dated temple inscriptions to the existing place account while preserving visitor-access uncertainty. See [Jagannath temple, Puri](../places/jagannath-temple-puri.md), [Chodaganga](../people/anantavarman-chodaganga.md) and [Anangabhima III](../people/anangabhima-deva-iii.md).

## Next evidence to recover

The University of Pennsylvania lists David Gold’s **2002 critical edition and translation of the Tirthacintamani’s Samanya, Prayaga and Purusottama sections**. Its full text has not been read. [University record](https://www.southasia.upenn.edu/graduate/phds). UT Austin also identifies the 1912 Smrititirtha edition and links a scan; its apparatus still needs inspection. Neither a catalogue entry nor the Tagare translation completes the critical-edition requirement.

Next inspect those editions, the Ganga charter construction passages and a critically edited Madala Panji. For livelihoods, seek dated temple accounts, procurement, service-role and craft-household evidence. Keep worshippers, visits, meals, workers and sales in separate units. Current visitor rules remain a separate unresolved operating check.

# Khalkatapatna: a medieval international connection

The 2015 research note associates Khalkatapatna with thirteenth–fifteenth-century contacts with China and Arabia. Its field observations include ceramics and ring wells exposed by riverbank erosion.[^maritime-khalkatapatna]

## Meaning

Use the site as evidence of a trading landscape, not as a proxy for an ancient national trade total. “Arabia” is a historical regional attribution; do not silently convert it into the modern UAE, Saudi Arabia or another single country.

## Next evidence

Obtain the excavation catalogue, specimen identifiers, ceramic provenance and date ranges. The published note’s wording varies between sections on the precise activity window; keep a broad medieval description until harmonised.

[China’s modern export share](../trade/export-destinations.md) is a separate observation that can appear alongside this history.

[^maritime-khalkatapatna]: [Khalkattapatna port: the lost archaeological heritage of Odisha, east coast of India](https://drs.nio.res.in/drs/bitstream/handle/2264/4813/Curr_Sci_109_372.pdf?isAllowed=y&sequence=1)

body:
# A stone anchor connects Odisha and Gujarat

Tripati and colleagues analysed a broken medieval-type anchor found at Manikapatna using petrography, chemistry and isotopes. They identified Palitana-area Deccan basalt in Gujarat as its most likely rock source.[^maritime-anchor]

## Why it matters

This is a material-provenance connection, stronger than a resemblance-based cultural claim. It supports investigating movement across the Indian coastal network. The finding does not identify a ship, crew, itinerary or traded cargo quantity.

## Marketing treatment

“A stone with a journey to tell.” Show the object only with correct attribution and image rights; animate the relationship as probable provenance, not a reconstructed sailing track.

[Manikapatna context](manikapatna.md) · [Trade evidence](maritime-evidence.md)

[^maritime-anchor]: [Geochemical provenance of an Indo-Arabian stone anchor from Manikapatna highlights the medieval maritime trade of India](https://www.vliz.be/imisdocs/publications/381044.pdf)

# Manikapatna: overseas objects and a port site

The 2026 research abstract reports Chinese ceramics and Chinese and Sri Lankan coins at Manikapatna; it describes activity around the sixth–seventh through seventeenth centuries CE.[^maritime-manikapatna-2026]

The 2022 paper reports earlier excavation phases of second century BCE–fifth/sixth century CE and ninth–nineteenth century CE.[^maritime-anchor]

## Interpretation

These finds support a connected exchange setting. They do not by themselves measure shipment volume, establish the nationality of the carrier, or prove a nonstop bilateral route. The two chronological descriptions need reconciliation against excavation reports; preserve both rather than averaging them.

## Story use

Follow one documented object from its find context to its scholarly identification, then connect the place to a dated modern export observation. Explain the change of evidence type on screen.

[Anchor provenance](manikapatna-anchor.md) · [Modern destinations](../trade/export-destinations.md)

[^maritime-manikapatna-2026]: [Manikapatna: A Historical Period Port Site on the East Coast of Ancient Kalinga and its Maritime Relation with Southeast Asia](https://www.ippasecretariat.org/ippa2026/sessions/s07/s07-a5)

title: Maritime Odisha: the evidence structure
description: Maritime Odisha: the evidence structure — evidence, scope and reuse.
body:
# Maritime Odisha: the evidence structure

Odisha’s maritime story can be connected through objects, sites, commemorations and modern trade observations. Those links support an outward-looking commercial identity. They do not supply an ancient export ledger or a continuous company history.

## The strongest connected stories

| Connection | Historical or cultural anchor | Modern link | Claim boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| China | [Ceramic and coin finds](manikapatna.md), plus [Khalkatapatna](khalkatapatna.md) | [Export destination observation](../trade/export-destinations.md) | Archaeological circulation does not specify a direct sailing route |
| Sri Lanka | Reported coins at [Manikapatna](manikapatna.md) | Odisha-specific current trade value still needed | No invented modern total |
| Indonesia / Bali | [Commemoration](../culture/boita-bandana.md) and [India–Bali archaeological research](bali-and-indonesia.md) | Country-specific state export and buyer data still needed | Indian contact is not automatically Odisha-exclusive |
| Malay Peninsula | [Published route reconstruction](palur-and-bay-routes.md) | Malaysia appears in the export-destination table | Historical region and modern national territory are different |
| Gujarat | [Archaeometric provenance of an anchor](manikapatna-anchor.md) | Potential contemporary coastal-logistics research | Rock provenance is not a complete ship itinerary |
| Enterprise in Odisha | [Boita Bandana](../culture/boita-bandana.md) | [Paradip’s own commemoration](../trade/paradip-bridge.md) and [fair sales reporting](../trade/baliyatra-commerce.md) | Cultural pride is not a measured cause of business performance |

## A chronology with visible uncertainty

Read each site’s dated record separately. The 2022 Manikapatna paper’s archaeological phases and the 2026 conference abstract’s activity window are not identical. Neither should be converted into “uninterrupted global trade for 2,000 years.” Object dates, occupation dates and voyage dates are different variables.

## Geographic discipline

Use Utkal · Odisha as the campaign identity. In historical records, retain the source’s Kalinga, Utkal or Odra terminology and time-dependent geography. Do not assign every port of the wider historical east-coast network to today’s Odisha. Treat cultural transmission as a specific, testable proposition: which practice or object, at which place and date, with what evidence of direction?

## Reusable data

The [linked-data method](../methods/maritime-linked-data.md) explains the entity and claim graph. A missing number is stored as missing, never as zero. The [research queue](research-agenda.md) prioritises the remaining trade and historical joins.

body:
# Next evidence needed for a global trading story

## Highest-value joins

1. **Odisha → country → product → year:** obtain official state-of-origin exports at HS product-code level, in both value and quantity, for China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam and Sri Lanka. Retain state-of-origin methodology, revisions, currencies and complete annual series. This will identify real product relationships rather than relying on country-level symbolism.
2. **Product → producer → buyer:** identify public, attributable commercial examples in metals, seafood, textiles and food. Confirm actual shipments or contracts before treating plans or trade-fair meetings as outcomes.
3. **Festival → seller → sales:** obtain ORMAS and district closing reports, definitions of sales, participating-stall counts and event dates. Separate visitor entries from unique people; avoid economic-impact multipliers without a study.
4. **Object → excavation → origin:** retrieve Manikapatna and Khalkatapatna catalogues, accession identifiers, dating methods and museum locations. Ask a qualified archaeologist to review the proposed public claims.
5. **Inscription → transcription → translation:** pursue the Kling/Cane and related Javanese leads through original editions and current scholarship. Historical ethnonyms need contextual interpretation.
6. **Cultural influence:** investigate one named practice or object at a time with Indonesian and other regional scholarship. Similarity alone does not establish source, direction or exclusive authorship.

## Known issues to preserve

- Manikapatna chronology differs across the 2022 research paper and 2026 abstract.
- The 2019 Roman-contact paper’s discussion is substantially more cautious than its abstract.
- Export destination percentages need underlying-table denominator reconciliation before conversion into rupee values.
- The survey’s marine-destination Figure 4.9 contains an unresolved editorial note about quantity versus value; do not substitute those shares for the overall export-destination table.
- The 2024 fair-sales article has inconsistent title metadata and lacks an audited closing statement.

## Measurement plan

For future campaigns, track qualified enquiries, maker referrals, completed purchases, export leads progressing to confirmed orders and visitor bookings with consented attribution. Set a baseline before launch. Historical content is an entry point; business outcomes need contemporary measurement.

This is a research queue, not evidence that ancient trade volumes, trader counts or market shares are known. The initial maritime module is not an exhaustive archive of all Odisha history.

The 2019 reassessment questions several supposed Roman finds and concludes that direct Odisha–Roman maritime contact lacks tangible support in the evidence reviewed. Indirect exchange remains a possibility.[^maritime-romans-2019]

Its abstract can sound stronger than its conclusion. Read the discussion on pages 1394–1395 before citing the paper. Do not use “Odisha traded directly with Rome” as an established headline on the basis of this source.

This does not negate Odisha’s wider maritime history. It identifies which particular route claim is unresolved. Keep this record discoverable so future marketing research does not repeatedly pick up the stronger, unsupported version.

The paper also distinguishes historical names and changing boundaries. That supports retaining historical geography separately from present-day state identity.

body:
# Scientific knowledge preserved in manuscripts

Odisha’s manuscript heritage gives the science timeline a second route: follow surviving catalogue records alongside biographies. The museum’s undated department page describes approximately 37,000 manuscripts across 27 categories, including mathematics, astronomy/astrology and medicine. Its separate collection table gives 37,273. Neither is a current science-manuscript count or a measure of unique works. The pages provide no common inventory date, so no change is calculated. [Department](https://odishamuseum.nic.in/?q=dept/manuscripts); [collection table](https://www.odishamuseum.nic.in/?q=node/5).

## Bhāsvatī beyond Odisha

IGNCA’s 2024 catalogue, printed p.102, records *Bhāsvatī* witnesses at BORI in Pune, Kamarupa Anusandhan Samiti in Guwahati and Saraswati Bhawan Library in Varanasi. Four selected entries retain catalogue identifiers, folio counts, completeness and scripts in the [evidence register](../references/data/science-heritage.json). The Guwahati entry credits a commentary to Karirāja Cakravarti. These are catalogue descriptions of manuscripts represented in IGNCA’s microfilm collection, not four independent historical studies. [Catalogue](https://ignca.gov.in/PDF_data/Jyotish-Vol-6-Part-1.pdf#page=120).

This extends the [Bhāsvatī work record](../works/bhasvati.md) with institutional catalogue evidence. Repository locations demonstrate documented preservation beyond Odisha; they do not establish when the text travelled, its influence abroad or a continuous scientific institution. The work’s composition date and a surviving copy’s date are different fields. Unspecified Saṁvat dates remain unconverted.

## Mathematics on palm leaf

The museum’s [Ganita catalogue](https://odishamuseum.nic.in/?field_abstraction_tid=All&field_author_value=&field_category_tid=All&field_subject_value=&page=1&q=palm-leaf-g) lists *Lilabati Pati Ganita* (G/141), *Ganita Chautisha* (G/43) and *Khadi Pothi* (G/112) as palm-leaf records. Their displayed author fields are blank. Names, dates, language interpretation and intellectual content need manuscript-level checks before these can become credited scientist profiles. A title containing a poetic form offers a research lead for science and literary expression, not proof of a particular teaching practice.

## What remains open

INSA’s bibliography confirms Deepak Bhattacharya’s eight-page 2008 survey in *Indian Journal of History of Science* 43(1), pp.101–108. The full survey could not be retrieved; its table entries remain unverified leads. [Publisher index](https://insaindia.res.in/history-of-science/).

The Devīdāsa commentary lead in the already saved Panda study still needs an identifiable manuscript record. No new early scientist has been inferred from surname, text title or custody alone. Original folios, colophons, acquisition histories and specialist attribution remain the next evidence layer. Museum scanning and online catalogue presence do not establish complete digitisation, public full-text access or reuse rights.

[Scientific heritage timeline](../people/science-and-contributions.md) — Read manuscript records alongside named contributors; collection custody does not establish an author’s Odisha origin.

# Odisha FDI index — recorded inflows and trends

**Current use:** Background reference. The user replaced the standalone FDI focus with [Investment in Odisha](investment.md). The weekly agent no longer monitors this as an independent headline track. The saved numbers were rechecked against DPIIT Table 5 on 27 September 2026; the USD-million units are confirmed.

## The reader’s takeaway

**US$69.72 million of FDI equity inflows recorded in 2025.**

The comparable calendar-year figures were **US$11.83 million in 2023** and **US$4.41 million in 2024**. The 2025 rise was **US$65.31 million**, or approximately **15.8 times** the 2024 amount, from a small base.[^journey-fdi-mar2026]

## Index scope

This is an organised tracker of official **FDI equity inflows**, not a new composite investment-attractiveness score. DPIIT’s state detail covers the equity component; it is not total FDI including reinvested earnings and other capital.[^journey-fdi-mar2026]

## The saved time windows

- **2023:** US$11.83 million.
- **2024:** US$4.41 million.
- **2025:** US$69.72 million.
- **January–March 2026:** US$14.68 million; a partial year.
- **October 2019–March 2026:** reported cumulative US$257.19 million, also reported as ₹2,054.88 crore.[^journey-fdi-mar2026]

All figures above are recorded as assigned to Odisha in the cited DPIIT table. The three full-year observations are calendar years. The table pools October 2019–December 2022 into one US$156.54-million cell; that cell is not an annual observation.

## Meaning and presentation

Show the three complete years as directly labelled bars beginning at zero. Put the 2026 partial-year value on a separate card. Prefer “FDI equity inflows rebounded in 2025” with the absolute values visible. A 15.8× headline alone would overstate the breadth of evidence by concealing the small base.

Use the source’s reported INR and USD values; do not treat their ratio as a current exchange rate. Keep investment summits, domestic project proposals, approved project costs and announced foreign interest in a separate pipeline collection.

## Calculation and scope notes

The year-on-year percentage change is derived from the displayed rounded source inputs. The table’s rounded component periods sum to US$257.18 million, while it reports US$257.19 million cumulatively. Retain the reported cumulative figure and the US$0.01-million rounding difference. The underlying unrounded observations are unavailable here.

No five- or ten-year growth rate, comprehensive state ranking or sector/investor attribution is established by this short series. The source ends in March 2026; this record does not claim it is the latest release available in September 2026. A newer-release check is part of the research queue.

# Investment in Odisha — domestic and foreign capital

## The current editorial focus

**Investment in Odisha — domestic and foreign capital, from commitment to operation.** The user replaced the standalone FDI headline track on 27 September 2026. Present values in ₹ crore or ₹ lakh crore, with stage and period beside every number. The [saved FDI series](fdi.md) remains a narrow reference, not the weekly headline.

## A supported starting point

| Measure | Period | Officially reported amount | Meaning |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 80 industrial projects described as implemented | 2025 | ₹1.75 lakh crore | Investment associated with reported implementation; cash-spend definition not established |
| 244 approved industrial projects | 2025 | ₹5.66 lakh crore | Estimated project budgets; approval does not establish expenditure |

These two values come from section 5.1.3 of the full survey's official indexed passage.[^investment-survey-full-2026] The executive summary gives less precise versions, ₹1.7 lakh crore and ₹5.6 lakh crore. Preserve both publication variants rather than treating their difference as new investment.[^investment-survey-summary-2026]

The summary also records ₹15.1 lakh crore of commitments across 275 MoUs at listed 2025 investor events, and ₹65,010 crore of state capital outlay in FY2025–26 budget estimates. These are separate coverage and status measures.[^investment-survey-summary-2026]

## What we can say

**“Odisha reports ₹1.75 lakh crore in investment across 80 industrial projects implemented in 2025.”** Attribute this to the Economic Survey and retain its implementation terminology. This is stronger evidence than an intent-only headline, but it is not an audited statewide total of cash spent or proof that every plant is operating.

The figures do not supply a domestic/foreign funding split. They are a broader industrial-investment starting point that is not restricted to the DPIIT foreign-equity series. Do not label their sum as total domestic plus foreign investment.

## Tracker design

Maintain three reader-facing views: **investment delivered**, **projects progressing**, and **future commitments**. Put an actual expenditure figure in the first view only when source scope and period support it. Keep reported implementation with its source label until commissioning or expenditure is established.

For each project capture a stable project ID, promoter, district, sector, ownership/funding origin when documented, phase, stage date, announced/approved cost, cumulative and period spending if disclosed, commissioned capacity and employment status. Unknown fields remain unknown. Match repeated announcements and expansion phases before aggregation.

Track private businesses, public-sector enterprises and government capital outlay separately. Domestic/foreign/mixed ownership and public/private ownership are different classifications. Corporate headquarters, promoter nationality or a foreign brand name do not by themselves measure how a project was financed.

Do not add MoUs, approved costs and implemented-project amounts: the same projects may appear in multiple stages. Do not add FDI flows to project costs, or cumulative capital stock to annual spending. Exclude growth/conversion rates until comparison coverage and project cohorts match. A comprehensive statewide realised investment total has not yet been established.

## Next evidence to obtain

IPICOL and Industries Department project-level implementation definitions and lists; company annual reports/exchange filings with Odisha-specific capital expenditure; commissioning evidence; Finance Accounts and budget actuals for public capital outlay; comparable five/ten-year series. Use successive releases to build evidence, not to inflate the same project's total.

[Structured seed tracker](../references/data/investment-tracker.json) · [Weekly runbook](../methods/weekly-data-agent.md)


[^investment-survey-full-2026]: [Odisha Economic Survey 2025–26, section 5.1.3](https://assembly.odisha.gov.in/WriteReadData/News/OES%202026%20WEB%20UPLOAD.pdf)

[^investment-survey-summary-2026]: [Odisha Economic Survey 2025–26, executive summary: industrial investment and capital outlay](https://pc.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2026-02/ES-Highlights%20and%20Executive%20Summary%202026%20Web%20Upload.pdf)

## Tourism application evidence

The [tourism policy opportunity brief](../collections/tourism-policy-opportunity.md) tracks the new portal announcement and guidance gaps. Keep tourism incentive applications, sanctions, disbursements and operating outcomes separate, following the stage distinctions above. The proposed [experience pilot](../../specs/tourism-experience-pilot.md) tests local delivery; it is not an investment or subsidy award.

# Odisha’s rare-earth journey

## The reader’s takeaway

**An existing processing base, with a new corridor ambition.**

IREL lists **11,200 tonnes per year of installed mixed rare-earth chloride capacity** at OSCOM in Odisha. That is plant capacity, not measured annual output or pure rare-earth oxide tonnage.[^journey-irel-reep]

## Milestones

- **1986:** IREL commissioned the OSCOM mining and mineral-separation unit at Chatrapur.[^journey-irel-history]
- **FY2015–16:** IREL’s plant profile dates commissioning of its rare-earth extraction plant to this financial year.[^journey-irel-reep]
- **Union Budget 2026–27:** Odisha was named alongside Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu for proposed dedicated rare-earth corridors. An April 2026 parliamentary reply said a joint working group was being constituted to develop guidelines.[^journey-rare-corridor]

- **11 August 2026:** a ministerial meeting discussed an integrated science roadmap linking the proposed corridor with marine biotechnology and other research. This release does not establish corridor commissioning or new plant output.[^weekly-rare-aug2026]

## Meaning and presentation

Show two clearly labelled layers: **established facilities** and **proposed expansion**. A simple value-chain illustration can explain mineral extraction, chemical processing and downstream manufacturing, but each stage needs its own location and evidence. IREL’s company profile places high-purity oxide refining at Aluva in Kerala; do not label the entire company value chain as located in Odisha.[^journey-irel-history]

The story opportunity is Odisha’s role in higher-value materials. Do not equate all beach-sand minerals with rare earths, or connect rare-earth projects to Odisha semiconductor projects as a confirmed supply relationship without evidence.

## What to track next

Plant-level output and capacity utilisation over time; product basis; Odisha-specific resource estimates with dates and methodology; corridor guidelines, named projects, spending and commissioning; downstream buyers and processing locations; environmental permissions and operating safeguards relevant to each facility.

The corporate page’s approximate 11,000-tonne description and the plant page’s 11,200-tpa figure have different precision. This record uses the specific plant figure and does not sum them.

# Odisha’s semiconductor journey

## The reader’s takeaway

**Two Odisha projects approved under the India Semiconductor Mission in August 2025.**

SiCSem covers silicon-carbide compound semiconductors; 3D Glass Solutions covers advanced packaging and embedded glass substrates. Approval identifies a developing pipeline, not two factories already producing commercially.[^legacy-ism]

## Milestones

- **12 August 2025 — approval:** the Union Cabinet approved SiCSem and 3D Glass Solutions projects in Odisha. SiCSem’s planned annual capacity was 60,000 wafers.[^legacy-ism]
- **19 April 2026 — groundbreaking:** the HIPS/3D Glass project at Info Valley reached its foundation-stone event. Reported project investment: **₹1,943.53 crore**. Commercial production was targeted for August 2028, with full-volume production targeted for August 2030.[^legacy-glass]
- **15 September 2026 — separate SEZ approval:** SiCSem’s proposal recorded **₹3,406.25 crore** investment and approximately **1,270 expected jobs**. These remain a proposal value and employment projection.[^legacy-sicsez]
- **18 September 2026 — wider pipeline:** MeitY reported approximately **₹23,600 crore of investment proposals**, 6,100 potential employment opportunities and an announced 870-acre Odisha Silicon Valley at Naraj. These are ecosystem proposals and an announced development.[^journey-semicon-2026]

## Meaning and presentation

Use a milestone ribbon with explicit labels: **approved → groundbreaking → construction evidence → commissioned → commercial production**. Put future targets on a visibly separate timeline. A later approval can concern an existing project rather than a new factory.

Do not add the broad September proposal total to named project estimates: overlap has not been reconciled. Do not add SiCSem’s separate approval figures as if each were additional investment. Keep planned jobs, realised headcount, installed capacity and actual output in separate fields.

The earlier [SiCSem evidence records](../evidence/s02.md) use another approval-context investment figure; its scope difference from the SEZ proposal remains unresolved. The [saved RIR update](../evidence/s11.md) remains a secondary account pending the underlying company filing. The new primary sources checked here do not establish commercial output at those facilities.

## What to track next

Project-specific construction and commissioning evidence; production-start disclosures; actual spending; employment; local supplier links; skills programmes and outcomes. Preserve the distinction between manufacturing, packaging, design and training.
