body:
# Beyond the metal: Odisha’s small suppliers

An industrial story need not stop at a mine or a plant. Ask who supplies the goods and services that keep the work moving. That question opens a door towards smaller businesses—and towards the records that can connect a company’s purchasing to a particular enterprise.

NALCO’s reports provide a starting point. They identify procurement from Odisha-based micro and small enterprises (MSEs). The figures show a business connection worth investigating; they do not yet tell us a supplier’s profit, a worker’s pay or a family’s experience.

## A local connection, with its denominator visible

For **FY2025–26**, NALCO reports **₹652.19 crore** in goods and services purchases from Odisha-based MSEs, within **₹1,447.94 crore** from MSEs across locations. The Odisha-based portion is about **45.04% of that MSE total**. It is not a share of all company purchases. “Odisha-based” describes the supplier location in the disclosure; it does not prove where every purchased item was manufactured. [Annual report, printed p.56 / PDF p.76, section19(a)](https://nalcoindia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/45th-Annual-Report-2025-26.pdf).

The preceding report year gives the comparison another dimension.

| NALCO reporting year | Purchases from Odisha-based MSEs, ₹ crore | Purchases from all-location MSEs, ₹ crore | Odisha-based share of this MSE total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FY2024–25 | 570.46 | 898.76 | 63.47% |
| FY2025–26 | 652.19 | 1,447.94 | 45.04% |

The earlier values come from NALCO’s sustainable-development report, printed p.41 / PDF p.43. Shares are our calculations from the displayed purchase values, rounded to two decimal places. Both publications have corporate provenance; two report editions are not independent corroboration. [FY2024–25 report](https://nalcoindia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/NALCO-SD-Report-2025-Final.pdf).

**The reported Odisha-based value rose, while its share of the MSE total fell.** Those statements can both be true because the denominator also changed. Neither establishes the cause, the number of businesses benefiting or higher household incomes. The reports’ separate policy-related procurement percentages answer a different denominator question and should not replace the location shares above.

## Follow the paper trail towards one enterprise

To turn this aggregate into a human story, begin with an actual supplier and its work. The following is a reporting path, not a description of a contract we have verified:

| Stage to investigate | Evidence to look for | What it cannot establish alone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry | Dated registration and enterprise classification | That the business received an order |
| Award | Named purchase order or contract with value and scope | That work was completed or paid |
| Delivery | Completion or acceptance record | The supplier’s margin or household income |
| Payment and experience | Invoice/payment evidence and permitted participant account | A statewide benefit from one case |

A supplier could explain a difficult specification, the work behind a delivery or what receiving payment meant. These are questions for future reporting. No supplier interview, award, receipt or endorsement has been collected for this draft.

## Keep neighbouring industrial cases separate

The [bauxite-to-aluminium case](../economy/bauxite-to-aluminium.md) supplies NALCO’s wider industrial context. [Rourkela’s steel case](../economy/rourkela-steel-chain.md) follows another plant and another evidence trail. Its recorded purchase-order measure must remain separate from NALCO’s procurement figures; adding them would not produce a verified Odisha total.

For a later visual treatment, show each financial year’s MSE total as a separately labelled bar, divided by supplier location. Print the total and the Odisha-based amount beside each. Do not use equal-length share bars alone if the point is to show both amount and share. A supplier photograph would need an identified business, permission and usable rights; a generic factory image cannot stand in for their testimony.

The invitation is to look beyond the finished metal. A purchasing figure can point towards a business relationship. A carefully evidenced enterprise story can help us understand the work within it.

<details>
<summary>Evidence and editorial scope</summary>

Original procurement passages in the two NALCO PDFs were retrieved and visually checked on 11 October 2026. The [mining research](../economy/mining.md) retains company, workforce, supplier and community questions separately. Comparisons here use reported nominal purchase values; no inflation adjustment, jobs multiplier, supplier-profit estimate or causal household outcome is supplied. Other original source records remain dated evidence, not newly confirmed awards. This remains a KB editorial draft; no independent human review, current supplier opportunity or website release is claimed.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Earlier research draft, preserved</summary>

**₹652.19 crore in purchases from Odisha-based micro and small enterprises.** That is what NALCO reports for 2025–26, giving the mineral economy a concrete connection to smaller businesses.

The company reports ₹1,447.94 crore in total purchases from MSEs across locations. Odisha-based suppliers therefore account for **about 45% of this MSE total**. This is procurement of goods and services, not supplier profit, jobs created or a share of all company purchasing. [NALCO annual report, printed p.56, section 19(a)](https://nalcoindia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/45th-Annual-Report-2025-26.pdf).

A simple proposed visual: one bar split into 45% Odisha-based MSE purchases and 55% other MSE purchases. Label the denominator and year directly. Pair it with a credited supplier’s story only after finding a named enterprise and evidence for its actual work; no interview or participant endorsement is claimed.

[The bauxite-to-aluminium chain](../economy/bauxite-to-aluminium.md) explains the industrial context. [Rourkela’s steel case](../economy/rourkela-steel-chain.md) asks the same questions of another industry, without assigning NALCO’s supplier results to it.

[Mining research](../economy/mining.md) — Connects plant and supplier evidence to the broader mining programme without equating company results with household benefits.

## What can be compared

NALCO’s FY2024–25 report records ₹570.46 crore from Odisha-based MSEs within ₹898.76 crore from all MSEs. Preserve these alongside the following year’s figures, with report editions and denominators visible. Supplier location does not prove where goods were manufactured. [Earlier-year source](../sources/mining-nalco-sd2025.md).

Rourkela’s ₹133.46 crore disclosure measures purchase orders placed on Odisha-based LSSIs. It is a separate measure, so we do not combine it with NALCO’s purchases into an Odisha total. [RSP source](../sources/mining-rsp-subplac2026.md).

For a named supplier story, the next evidence needs are an actual award or order, the enterprise’s location and classification at that date, and a paid-invoice or completion record. A tender invitation or vendor registration alone cannot establish business received. No supplier interview or endorsement is claimed.

</details>

body:
# Odisha’s ferrochrome reaches industrial markets abroad

Not every connection with the world arrives as a recognisable object on a shop shelf. An industrial material can travel through a chain of businesses, leaving its clearest trace in a company’s market and sales records. Reading that trace offers another way to be curious about Odisha’s place in trade.

IMFA’s FY2025–26 report offers one such case. Its customer description places ferrochrome within the stainless-steel manufacturing chain, with industrial buyers and trading intermediaries. That is a different kind of connection from a consumer brand becoming famous abroad. [Annual report, printed p.58 / PDF p.31](https://www.imfa.in/api/pdf/IMFAAnnualReportFY2526.pdf/IMFA_Annual_Report_FY_2526_10bbee90f9.pdf).

## Read two movements, not one success label

The report’s domestic and international sales rows move in different directions: domestic tonnes rise, while international tonnes ease. Keep both visible. A single export headline would leave out part of the business story; a single domestic-growth headline would do the same.

The preserved evidence panel below gives the reported values and scope. Market reach, physical sales and export turnover share answer different questions. Counting country markets does not tell us how sales are distributed among them; a turnover percentage does not supply a tonnes percentage. These distinctions matter before drawing a map or giving the story a dramatic caption.

## The dated company evidence

**13 country markets served in FY2025–26.** IMFA’s standalone disclosure gives Odisha’s mineral-processing story a measurable trade connection. Exports accounted for 85.47% of company turnover. These are company measures, not statewide exports or a measure of global popularity. [Annual report, p.58](https://www.imfa.in/api/pdf/IMFAAnnualReportFY2526.pdf/IMFA_Annual_Report_FY_2526_10bbee90f9.pdf).

A proposed two-panel visual would show domestic sales rising from 34,066 to 48,769 tonnes and international sales easing from 225,801 to 221,355 tonnes between FY2024–25 and FY2025–26. Keep both panels on the same scale. Sales volume and export turnover share use different denominators.

The [company chain](../economy/company-imfa.md) connects captive chromite mines, Odisha processing facilities and industrial buyers. It also preserves what remains unknown: plant-specific jobs, local supplier purchases and current commissioning status beyond the report date.

[Mining research](../economy/mining.md) — Connects a company trade example to Odisha’s broader mineral-processing research without treating it as a statewide total.

## Follow the material without inventing its journey

For a later visual, begin with two paired sales panels using the same scale and labelled financial years. A separate card can carry the country-market count and its company scope. This keeps quantity, reach and money apart rather than making unlike measures appear interchangeable.

A map needs named, documented destinations. The aggregate country count does not supply them. A mine-to-plant-to-customer graphic would need traceable relationships and reporting dates for each connection; we should not draw an exact cargo route from a company total. An evocative port photograph also needs a verified location and rights, and cannot prove this material travelled through that port.

A fuller human account could follow someone’s part in production, testing, logistics or a customer relationship. Start with an actual role and permission to tell the story, then check the supporting record. What work did the person do? What evidence connects it to the product? Which details are their experience, and which are company disclosures? These are reporting questions, not conversations we have conducted.

The [small-supplier story](minerals-and-local-suppliers.md) offers a neighbouring question: what evidence connects industrial purchasing to a particular business? Read it alongside this trade case, keeping the companies and measures distinct.

<details>
<summary>Evidence and editorial scope</summary>

The original report’s printed p.40 / PDF p.22 sales table and printed p.58 / PDF p.31 market and customer disclosure were visually checked on 11 October 2026. The measures remain company-reported; this inspection is not independent assurance. Existing mine-production reconciliation, plant allocations, local suppliers and worker outcomes remain open in the company record. # Odisha’s Best-Kept Secret — The Art of Cooking with Fire — campaign draft

## Campaign direction

**Odisha’s Best-Kept Secret**

*The Art of Cooking with Fire*

The user selected this campaign tag and subtitle on 1 October 2026. “Best-kept secret” is evocative editorial language, not a measured claim about awareness. Introduce poda within the story and explain the different cooking methods. Campaign wording approval does not establish factual review, media rights or website publication approval.

## Reader-facing story draft

Start with a vegetable, and follow the heat. Baigana poda turns roasted eggplant into a mustard-scented mash; tomato poda brings another roasted accompaniment to the table. Move to the parcels: mushrooms and fish seasoned and folded into leaves, or prawns charred inside sal leaves. Each wrapper makes the opening part of the meal. [Vegetable account](../food/baigana-poda.md), [tomato account](../food/tomato-poda.md), [mushroom and fish](../sources/food-patrapoda-lopa2024.md), [prawns](../food/chingudi-patrapoda.md).

Then widen the story. A historical Odisha Tourism menu describes leaf-cooked chicken; published reporting connects Odisha’s baunsa poda mansa with meat cooked inside bamboo. These are invitations to meet and credit the cooks behind each preparation, with local details still to document. [Chicken evidence](../food/kukuda-patrapoda.md), [bamboo evidence](../food/baunsa-poda-mansa.md).

The finish can be sweet. Poda pitha brings rice and festival memories; chhena poda brings fresh cheese and a browned surface. Roasted, wrapped or baked, the connection runs across ingredients and courses. **Discover the many ways Odisha cooks.** [Pitha](../food/poda-pitha.md), [cheese sweet](../food/chhena-poda.md).

## Short video script · draft

Estimated 35–45 seconds; not recorded or timed with the user’s clone.

“In Odisha, follow one word: poda. Start with roasted eggplant. Add tomato, sharp with mustard oil. Open a leaf parcel: mushrooms, fish or prawns. Follow the story to chicken in leaves and meat cooked inside bamboo. Then stay for dessert: poda pitha and chhena poda. Roasting, leaf cooking, slow baking—different methods, a delicious connection. Odisha’s best-kept secret: the art of cooking with fire.”

Visual sequence proposal: vegetable roasting → opening a leaf parcel → a credited bamboo-cooking demonstration → slicing pitha and chhena poda. Use consented, correctly labelled footage of the actual method. An oven-baked example must not be presented as a filmed ember preparation. Media and music rights remain unestablished; no video has been generated.

## Poster copy · draft

ODISHA’S BEST-KEPT SECRET

The Art of Cooking with Fire

From roasted vegetables and leaf-wrapped delicacies to caramelised sweets—discover Odisha’s poda traditions.

## Editorial evidence controls

The [nine-entry evidence collection](../food/poda-and-fire-cooking.md) distinguishes source types, methods and unresolved fields. The linked draft is a proposed tasting narrative, not a traditional fixed menu or an available tour. Do not claim “everything is barbecued”, oldest/largest/best in India, uniquely Odishan leaf cooking, or a common origin for all these foods. Enduri’s steaming and modern enclosed/oven adaptations stay distinct. No recipe testing, human factual review, measured audience response or publication approval is claimed.

## Website adaptation · 1 October 2026

“Odisha cooks with fire” is the proposed website collection title, drawing on this campaign direction. The earlier selected campaign wording remains above. The first candidate uses three real, licensed photographs and links three preparation stories to a saved food-reading journey. No video or bookable tasting tour is implied. See the [collection data](../food/fire-cooking-stories.json).

body:
# Bhubaneswar beyond the rank: reading the 2025 university evidence

A city can live in the imagination through its stone, its food and the journeys people make to it. A university adds another question: what might someone become here? For Bhubaneswar, a pair of entries in a national ranking offers a doorway into that question. The numbers invite attention; reading them carefully gives the story its substance.

## Two names, one dated comparison

In the **2025 NIRF University category**, Siksha O Anusandhan (SOA) ranked **15**, and Kalinga Institute of Industrial Technology (KIIT) ranked **17**. Both are listed in Bhubaneswar, Odisha. These are 2025 category results, not a claim about the latest ranking or every institution in the city. [NIRF 2025 University table](https://www.nirfindia.org/Rankings/2025/UniversityRanking.html).

The small surprise appears when we put two editions beside each other.

| Institution | 2024 score | 2024 rank | 2025 score | 2025 rank |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SOA | 62.61 | 14 | 63.14 | 15 |
| KIIT | 62.53 | 15 | 62.87 | 17 |

**Both scores rose; both rank positions slipped.** A rank tells us a position in that edition’s comparison. A published score is a separate figure. Comparing two editions does not hold the ranking pool or method constant, or measure an individual student’s learning. The table cannot establish a causal improvement or decline in teaching. [NIRF 2024 University table](https://www.nirfindia.org/Rankings/2024/UniversityRanking.html) · [2025 table](https://www.nirfindia.org/Rankings/2025/UniversityRanking.html).

That is a useful habit to carry beyond this story: ask what the number describes before deciding what it means.

## Follow a graduating class

Now turn from the ranking year to a different clock: **the academic year in which a cohort graduated**. The institutions’ 2025 submissions contain earlier placement and higher-study tables. For their **2023–24 four-year undergraduate programmes**, the reported figures are:

| Institution | Graduated in minimum stipulated time | Placed | Selected for higher studies | Median annual salary among placed graduates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SOA | 2,471 | 2,218 | 237 | ₹6.00 lakh |
| KIIT | 3,611 | 3,513 | 98 | ₹9.70 lakh |

These are institution-submitted figures across four-year UG programmes, not engineering-only outcomes, an independent employment audit or pay for all graduates. The salary column is a **median among those placed**, not an average or a promise to a future applicant. The graduation column counts students finishing in the minimum stipulated time; it is not an entering-class count. [SOA submission, PDF p.2](https://www.nirfindia.org/nirfpdfcdn/2025/pdf/University/IR-O-U-0363.pdf) · [KIIT submission, PDF p.2](https://www.nirfindia.org/nirfpdfcdn/2025/pdf/University/IR-O-U-0356.pdf).

For KIIT, the same submission reports 4,021 placed graduates for 2021–22 and 3,513 for 2023–24, while the minimum-time graduation counts fall from 4,162 to 3,611. The reported median rises from ₹9.00 lakh to ₹9.70 lakh across those different cohorts. A salary trend and a headcount trend can move in different directions; neither tracks the same people over time. [KIIT submission, PDF p.2](https://www.nirfindia.org/nirfpdfcdn/2025/pdf/University/IR-O-U-0356.pdf).

The people behind these rows deserve richer accounts. What did they study? Which work did they find meaningful? What happened after the first offer? Those are reporting questions, not interviews we have conducted.

## Read the city with curiosity

This evidence gives a reader a reason to explore Bhubaneswar’s learning institutions alongside its other stories. It does not choose a course for them. A useful next conversation with a student or graduate would begin with the programme, graduating year and actual experience, rather than a city-wide claim drawn from two institutions.

Before making an education decision, seek current programme recognition, costs and admissions information, and the scope behind any placement claim. We have not verified those here. The [universities and learning collection](../culture/universities-and-learning.md) explains institutional categories and wider research; it also retains the unresolved intake/admission scope issue in KIIT’s submission, which prevents treating these rows as completion or utilisation rates.

For a future visual treatment, keep the two clocks apart: paired 2024/2025 score markers with their rank labels, followed by a separately labelled 2023–24 cohort panel. The story’s connection is from comparison to people. A campus image would need a verified location and usable rights; no photograph or imagined student testimony is supplied by this draft.

<details>
<summary>Evidence and editorial scope</summary>

The four linked NIRF sources and the [canonical learning dataset](../references/data/culture-learning.json) underpin this dated comparison. Original rank rows and both four-year UG tables were checked on 11 October 2026. Current rankings, admissions, programme costs, independent employment evidence and student interviews remain separate work. Figures are reported nominal rupees per year, with no inflation adjustment. No statewide jobs estimate, return-on-investment comparison or campus-access promise follows from them. This remains a KB editorial draft; no human review or website publication is claimed.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Earlier research draft, preserved</summary>

**Two Bhubaneswar institutions appear in the top 20 of NIRF’s 2025 University category:** SOA at 15 and KIIT at 17. This is a dated, category-specific national comparison.

| Institution | 2024 rank / score | 2025 rank / score |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SOA | 14 /62.61 | 15 /63.14 |
| KIIT | 15 /62.53 | 17 /62.87 |

Both published scores rose slightly while rank positions slipped. Keep both facts visible. Ranking pools and methods can change; the differences do not prove a measured rise in teaching quality or graduate earnings. [2024 table](https://www.nirfindia.org/Rankings/2024/UniversityRanking.html) · [2025 table](https://www.nirfindia.org/Rankings/2025/UniversityRanking.html).

**Beyond rank: follow the graduate cohort.** In their 2025 submissions, the 2023–24 four-year undergraduate cohorts report median annual pay among placed graduates of ₹6 lakh at SOA and ₹9.7 lakh at KIIT. These are institution-reported aggregates across four-year programmes, not engineering-only salaries, all-graduate earnings or promises to applicants. [SOA table,p.2](https://www.nirfindia.org/nirfpdfcdn/2025/pdf/University/IR-O-U-0363.pdf) · [KIIT table,p.2](https://www.nirfindia.org/nirfpdfcdn/2025/pdf/University/IR-O-U-0356.pdf).

Suggested visual: two paired score markers, with year and rank below each; place cohort outcomes in a separate card so ranking year and graduation year cannot be confused. Detailed student counts belong in the optional evidence view.

[Universities and learning](../culture/universities-and-learning.md) explains legal categories, wider institutions and comparison limits. Draft for editorial review; no current admissions endorsement, human review or website publication.

[Related reading](../culture/universities-and-learning.md) — Explains legal categories, institutional scope and comparison limits.

</details>

title: What remains after growing the rice?
description: A historical regional case shows why crop value, defined costs and household income need different questions.

sources.title: Study of Cropping Pattern and Profitability Analysis of Major Crops of North Eastern Ghats Agro-Climatic Zone of Odisha

publication_scope: Repository article draft; not a website release
body:
# What remains after growing the rice?

**A harvest has a value. The work behind it has a cost.**

A field of rice can invite admiration long before anyone asks about its accounts. Yet a bigger harvest alone cannot tell us what a grower keeps. Follow one historical regional study through its definitions, and the difference becomes visible.

## One hectare, three figures

P. P. Sahoo, K. K. Sarangi and S. N. Mishra’s study, published in **March 2023**, reports this paddy case for Odisha’s **North Eastern Ghats agro-climatic zone**. Its paddy survey and valuation year remain unresolved; these are **not current statewide averages**.

| Reported measure | Rupees per hectare |
| --- | ---: |
| Gross value, including the by-product | ₹79,050.00 |
| C2 cost under the study’s definitions | ₹64,908.43 |
| Reported net income above C2 | ₹14,141.58 |

The gross value combines ₹72,750 for the main product with ₹6,300 for the by-product. Calling the whole sum a grain-sale payment would change what it measures.

## The work that has no separate wage slip

The study’s **C2** accounts for valued family labour, land and owned-capital costs as well as other cultivation costs. “Valued” matters: work can enter an economic account even when it does not produce a separate wage payment. The table assigns family labour ₹9,000 per hectare in this case.

A smaller cost boundary gives a larger remainder. The paper also reports ₹38,036.90 per hectare as *farm business income* after **A2**. That is a different measure from the ₹14,141.58 after C2. A2 itself includes items such as depreciation and owned inputs; it should not be retold as a cash-only budget.

The two remainders are not competing answers to one question. Read the cost definition before deciding what an income figure tells you.

## Carry a better question into the next story

For future reporting, begin with one crop and an agreed period. Ask what was received, which costs were paid, how family work and land were valued, and what records support the account. These are proposed questions, not interviews Utkal Project has conducted. A household’s total income would need a wider account than this crop calculation.

The [procurement-payment story](rice-procurement-payments.md) asks a related question at a different scale. Departmental payments and a regional per-hectare cost study cannot be combined into a present-day farm-profit estimate.

At the next meal, the rice on the plate can prompt more than a question about taste. It can also prompt interest in the work that made the harvest possible—and in how carefully we listen when someone explains what remained.

<details>
<summary>Sources, calculations and earlier draft</summary>

[Sahoo, Sarangi and Mishra, Economic Affairs 68(1), 469–477, March 2023](https://ndpublisher.in/countpdfdownload.php?id=5788&pdf=EAv68n1p.pdf), DOI 10.46852/0424-2513.1.2023.16. Original PDF retrieved 11 October 2026; methods on printed pp.470–471 read, and paddy Tables 5–7 on pp.473–474 rendered and visually checked. The overall sample is 120 farmers in six clusters; the paddy-specific sample is not explicit. The 2018–19 date for secondary context is not assigned to the paddy results.

₹72,750 + ₹6,300 = ₹79,050. Subtracting displayed C2 yields ₹14,141.57, one paisa below the table’s ₹14,141.58; we retain the reported value and flag the rounding difference. The table’s gross value includes by-products although the methods formula names the main product alone. The [canonical case](../references/data/rice-economy.json) preserves that definition difference, the C3 discrepancy and the excluded ragi ratio. No new cross-crop comparison or current valuation is inferred.

Creative direction: **Ahimanikya Satapathy**. Developed and reviewed by the current AI assistant. No independent economics or human review, interview, fieldwork or agronomic recommendation is claimed. Underlying research and unresolved fields remain unchanged.

### Earlier draft · 2 October 2026

**About ₹14,142 per hectare remained after the study’s C2 costs.** This is a historical regional case published in 2023, with the paddy survey year unresolved—not a current Odisha average.

| The case, per hectare | Reported amount |
| --- | ---: |
| Paddy and by-product value | ₹79,050 |
| C2 cost, including valued family labour and land | ₹64,908.43 |
| Reported net income above C2 | ₹14,141.58 |

[Original study, Tables 6–7](https://ndpublisher.in/countpdfdownload.php?id=5788&pdf=EAv68n1p.pdf). The one-paisa difference from subtracting the displayed rounded costs is retained in the evidence record. Values are nominal; valuation year is unknown.

The editorial lesson is straightforward: a bigger harvest or a higher sale value does not tell us what a farmer keeps. Future rice stories should connect output with actual receipts, paid costs, family labour and land.

[Related reading](../economy/rice-economy.md) — Connects the regional cost case with procurement, seed enterprises and unresolved payment scope.

[Related reading](../statistics/agriculture.md) — Keeps historical case values separate from statewide production trends.

</details>

title: Rice kept for taste, seed saved for tomorrow
description: A reader-facing story connecting culinary preferences, Tulasa Ghiuria’s seed keeping and a historical women-led seed enterprise.

sources.title: More than70 landraces of paddy varieties have been conserved by Tulasa
Preserving agrobiodiversity: socio-cultural and economic drivers of landrace conservation in Odisha, India
Women farmers take a significant step towards seed security in Odisha

publication_scope: Repository article draft; not a website release
body:
# Rice kept for taste, seed saved for tomorrow

Before asking what goes beside the rice, ask which rice is on the plate. That small question opens a different way into Odisha: through the food someone wants to keep cooking, the seed they choose to keep, and the work needed for another sowing.

A bowl can be a beginning rather than the end of a story. Follow it towards Koraput’s seed keepers and a women-led seed enterprise in Kalahandi, with a pause for the particular pleasures people associate with particular rice names.

## The rice someone wants to cook

In a study published in February 2026, Preeti Yadav and colleagues recorded culinary preferences among selected farming communities in western Odisha and Koraput. Participants associated Kalahans with kanika and pakhala, and Sapuri with popped rice for weddings. These are reported local uses, not rules for every kitchen. The names do not establish that two seed lots are genetically identical.[1]

The choice offers a question to carry into a conversation: what would change in this meal if another rice were used? Leave room for the cook’s answer. A flavour, a texture or a family occasion may matter in a way that a list of varieties cannot explain.

## Tulasa Ghiuria and the next sowing

An account hosted by the M. S. Swaminathan Research Foundation places Tulasa Ghiuria in Nuaguda, Kundura, Koraput. It describes her conserving more than 70 indigenous rice varieties and cultivating Kalajeera, Dangarbasumati and Machhakanta. The page credits first publication to 26 July 2022; it is a dated account of her work, not a current seed catalogue.[2]

Read the names slowly. They give the story a person and a place, and make seed conservation something more tangible than a broad appeal to save heritage. The next question is practical: how does a grower tell them apart, and what makes each worth keeping? Asking gives the person doing the work room to explain what a packet label cannot.

## Women producing seed in Kalahandi

There is another kind of rice story in Kalahandi. IRRI’s May 2020 report describes Adarsh Dharmagarh Women Farmers Services Producer Company. It reports that around 180 women produced about 350 tons of paddy seed in 2019. Pooja foundation seed was among the material supplied to growers.[3]

That is seed production, not a tally of rice sold for meals. The account concerns a seed enterprise; it does not establish present operation or members’ profit. Alongside conservation, it opens a separate question: who makes seed available for the next crop, and what work makes that possible?

## A conversation to bring home

You do not need to arrive with a catalogue of correct answers. At a meal, begin with the name used by the person serving it. If they are willing to talk, ask how they choose the rice for that dish and who taught them the preparation. A remembered difference is worth listening to without turning one household’s answer into a claim about an entire region.

If a grower or seed keeper chooses to share their knowledge, ask what they would like a visitor to understand. Agree on credit and permission before recording, photographing or publishing their words. A source profile is an introduction to someone’s work, not permission to visit their home or request seed.

For a notebook, keep four things together: the rice name as given, the broad place, the dish or use, and who shared the account with permission. Record questions alongside answers. A careful conversation can leave you with more than a souvenir: a reason to notice the next bowl differently.

## Continue reading

[Odisha’s rice collection](../food/rice-varieties.md) — Connects source-attributed names, food uses and historical cultivation without assuming identical seed accessions.

[Pakhala](../food/pakhala.md) follows one familiar meal into different preparations.

[Rice economics](../economy/rice-economy.md) — Separates seed production, grain sales and farmer returns.

## Sources and context

1. [Yadav and colleagues, 2026](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/sustainable-food-systems/articles/10.3389/fsufs.2026.1769950/full), methods 2.2 and Tables 6–7. Selected participants; not a statewide survey of kitchens. Health claims are not adopted here.
2. [MSSRF’s Tulasa account](https://www.mssrf.org/our-stories/more-than-70-landraces-of-paddy-varieties-have-been-conserved-by-tulasa). The foundation’s repost and its credited newspaper original are one source family.
3. [IRRI, 12 May 2020](https://news.irri.org/2020/05/women-farmers-take-significant-step.html). Historical enterprise report; proposed sales and expansion are not treated as completed outcomes.

Editorial direction: Ahimanikya Satapathy. Prepared with AI assistance from the existing project research and rechecked sources; no interview or field visit is claimed. [Editorial evidence and publication preparation](../../records/rice-story-evidence-2026-10-10.json).

body:
# The money moving through Odisha’s paddy procurement

**A payment total opens the story. A farmer’s own accounts would carry it further.**

Rice belongs to everyday life in Odisha. Behind the meal is another set of questions: how much paddy entered government procurement, what payments the department reported, and what a grower kept after the work of producing it. The figures below help with the first two questions. The third needs evidence closer to the farm.

## Read the quantity in two seasons

The Food Supplies & Consumer Welfare Department’s *Annual Activity Report 2025–2026* lists these paddy quantities for **KMS 2024–25**, the marketing-year record.[^rice-fscw2026]

| Season | Paddy procured, tonnes |
| --- | ---: |
| Kharif | 7,345,707 |
| Rabi | 1,918,528 |
| **Derived total** | **9,264,235** |

The total is about **92.64 lakh tonnes**, consistent with the report’s rounded KMS summary. This measures paddy procured through the reported system, rather than all rice produced in Odisha. Paddy and milled rice also need their own quantity definitions.

The seasonal farmer columns require a different kind of care. Someone may sell in both seasons. Adding the columns cannot tell us how many distinct people sold paddy over the year.

## Read what the payment includes

For that same **KMS 2024–25**, the department reports **₹28,718 crore paid as MSP plus input assistance**. MSP means minimum support price. Keep both parts of the payment category beside the headline.[^rice-fscw2026]

The earlier year’s payment figure in this report covers MSP alone. A percentage comparison between those two totals would combine a change in money with a change in what the money includes. The [rice-economy research](../economy/rice-economy.md) preserves the earlier-report disagreement and the arithmetic reconciliation.

There is a second boundary around the figures: the report gives **86.30 lakh tonnes** for the financial-year window **1 April 2024–31 March 2025**, alongside its separate KMS total. Those are different reporting windows, not two interchangeable answers to the same question.[^rice-fscw2026]

## Follow the money towards a household

A reported procurement payment can tell us about the scale of a public purchasing system. It does not tell us a farmer’s profit. We would need actual receipts, production costs, labour, land and the relevant season to understand what remained for a particular grower.

For future reporting, begin with a willing farmer’s account of one harvest. What was sold, when was payment received, what expenses had already been paid, and how does the household account for its own labour? These are proposed questions, not testimony collected by Utkal Project.

The existing [cost-and-income story](rice-income-after-costs.md) offers a historical regional example of why gross value and income after defined costs differ. It cannot be used to turn this statewide procurement payment into a current profit estimate.

The desire to understand Odisha’s rice economy begins at a familiar meal. It becomes more useful when we follow a figure far enough to know whose question it answers—and whose experience still needs to be heard.

<details>
<summary>Source, calculations and earlier draft</summary>

The original departmental report was recovered and PDF pages12,28,31 (printed10,26,29) visually inspected on 11 October 2026. Seasonal quantities add to9,264,235 tonnes; division by100,000 gives92.64235 lakh tonnes, displayed as92.64. The financial-year window and both payment category labels were checked in the source.

The canonical reconciliation retains a small difference between the reported combined payment and quantity multiplied by a common rate. No bank-settlement records, formal correction notice or explanation of that difference has been obtained. This article reports the department’s figure; it does not claim an audited payment total, timely payment to every farmer or a measured household-welfare outcome. The report’s promotional wellbeing language is not adopted as evidence of impact.

Creative direction: **Ahimanikya Satapathy**. Developed and reviewed by the current AI assistant. No independent economics or human review, interview, field visit or present-day entitlement advice is claimed. Earlier wording is retained below; the underlying research dataset and its held findings are preserved.

### Earlier draft · 2 October 2026

**₹28,718 crore in MSP and input assistance** was reported paid to paddy farmers for **KMS 2024–25**. That is the Food Supplies & Consumer Welfare Department’s combined payment figure. It is not farmer profit. [Annual report, printed p.29](https://foododisha.in/Download/annual-activity-glance-25-26.pdf).

The same report separates **7,345,707 tonnes in kharif** and **1,918,528 tonnes in rabi** in its detailed table: about **92.64 lakh tonnes across the marketing year**. Seasonal quantities can be added; seasonal farmer counts cannot be treated as unique annual people without removing overlap.

The combined payment is close to, but does not exactly equal, the detailed quantity multiplied by the common-paddy rate plus assistance. Settlement details remain unverified. The earlier year’s figure covers MSP alone, so a payment-growth percentage would mix categories.

[Related reading](../economy/rice-economy.md) — Explains the payment reconciliation and the difference between marketing and financial years.

[Related reading](../stories/rice-income-after-costs.md) — Explains why procurement payments do not measure farm profit.

</details>

[^rice-fscw2026]: [Food Supplies & Consumer Welfare: Annual Activity Report 2025–2026](https://foododisha.in/Download/annual-activity-glance-25-26.pdf), printed pp.10,26,29 / PDF pp.12,28,31. Seasonal quantities, KMS/FY scope and payment labels; publication date unstated. Original pages visually checked 11 October 2026. Departmental reporting, not an independent settlement audit.

body:
# More rice from each hectare: Odisha’s changing harvest

A bowl of rice is an everyday beginning. A harvest table opens a different doorway: how much land carried the crop, how much rice it yielded, and how uneven the journey was from one year to the next. Read together, those measures tell a more interesting story than a single rising number.

Odisha’s recorded rice yield was higher in 2023–24 than ten years earlier. Yet the last step in that same series went down. Progress across a decade and a difficult comparison with the previous year can both be true. The chart below keeps that tension visible.

## The harvest has three measures

Area tells us the recorded crop footprint. Yield tells us rice production per hectare. Output tells us the total rice quantity. They are connected, but each answers a different question. None of them tells us what an individual household kept after growing and selling its crop.

| Historical-table measure | 2013–14 | 2023–24 | How to read it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Total crop area, thousand hectares | 4,180 | 4,087 | A smaller recorded crop area across these endpoints |
| Rice yield, kg per hectare | 1,821 | 2,823 | More rice per hectare in the statewide measure |
| Rice production, thousand metric tonnes | 7,613 | 11,538 | More recorded rice output across these endpoints |

These are the historical table’s total columns, combining its Kharif and Rabi entries. Crop area is not a count of farms, people or unique landowners. The rice-output column must also stay separate from the table’s paddy-output column and from quantities purchased through procurement. [Odisha Agriculture Statistics 2023–24, printed p.90 / PDF p.96](https://agri.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2025-05/OAS%20A4.pdf).

## Keep the uneven years in the picture

**Rice yield was about 55% higher in 2023–24 than ten years earlier.** The same official historical table shows output up 51.6%, while rice crop area was 2.2% smaller. This is a description of recorded changes; it does not isolate their causes.

![Odisha rice output with every annual observation from 2012–13 to 2023–24](../references/figures/rice-output-trend.png)

The five-year comparison also shows higher output (+49.2%). But 2023–24 production fell 3.3% from 2022–23, and the chart retains the earlier setbacks. Starting-year conditions affect any endpoint comparison. [Source: Odisha Agriculture Statistics 2023–24, printed p.90](https://agri.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2025-05/OAS%20A4.pdf).

[Rice economics](../economy/rice-economy.md) connects the trend to procurement and the evidence needed to assess farmer returns. This is an editorial draft; source checking is not public-release approval.

[Related economics](../economy/rice-economy.md) — Connects statewide crop trends with economic definitions; higher yield alone does not establish higher farmer profit.

The ten-year comparison begins in 2013–14; the plotted series begins one year earlier. Choosing a different starting point changes the comparison. A story that shows only two endpoints would lose the setbacks along the way. Keeping every annual point helps the reader see both the longer change and the interruptions.

This table describes the result. It does not isolate the contribution of seeds, water, weather, labour or policy. Those explanations need additional evidence with a matching place, season and method. We should leave space for them without assigning a cause from the shape of a line.

## Follow the grain towards the household

A larger harvest raises another question: what happened after it was grown? The [farmer-return story](rice-income-after-costs.md) follows the distinction between receipts and costs. The [procurement-payment story](rice-procurement-payments.md) follows government purchasing records. They are neighbouring chapters, each with its own population, period and measure; their figures cannot simply be attached to a statewide yield trend.

For a future reported household account, begin with an actual grower’s permission and a named season. Document the crop area, harvested quantity, grain retained, quantity sold, realised price, expenses and timing of payment. Identify how family labour and owned land are treated in any cost calculation. Then let the person explain what mattered to them. These are reporting questions; no interview or farm inspection is claimed here.

The [seed-and-taste story](rice-kept-for-taste.md) opens a further door. A crop can matter for what people choose to cook and keep, as well as for its physical yield. Read that account in its own evidence scope, without turning a variety’s cultural value into an unmeasured price premium.

## A visual that earns its place

Keep the existing annual output chart, with years and units readable. A later companion could give area and yield their own aligned panels rather than overlaying unlike scales. Mark the comparison endpoints and the final-year decline. A verified, permitted harvest photograph can introduce the people and setting; it cannot establish a farm’s yield or stand for every Odisha grower. Avoid invented sacks, earnings or quoted voices used to dramatise the statistics.

<details>
<summary>Evidence and editorial scope</summary>

The original historical table, printed p.90 / PDF p.96, was downloaded and visually inspected on 11 October 2026. The ten-year yield, output and area changes and the final-year output decline were recalculated using the rounded historical values. The earlier draft and its chart are retained above; detailed-table precision variants remain in the canonical data. This is a dated statewide crop account, not a current harvest forecast, a causal evaluation or evidence of household profit. Procurement settlement and cost-study period gaps remain open in RES-061. Same-assistant editorial review is not independent human or farmer review. This KB draft does not change website content or search eligibility.

</details>

title: From milk to market: the work behind a sweet
description: A Pahala case study opens a reader journey through ingredients, making, distribution and the questions behind a sale.

Khordha District Census Handbook 2001 — town commodity directory
Dhenkanal Magji: attributed confectioner account
Sisir Saras 2026: Rasabali among featured products

publication_scope: Repository article draft; not a website release
body:
# From milk to market: the work behind a sweet

**The customer sees a sweet. Follow it backwards and a network of work appears.**

A rasagola offers a small invitation to look beyond the counter. Who supplied the chhena? Who brought it to the maker? Where did preparation end and selling begin? Those questions make food identity more tangible, connecting something familiar with work that is less visible.

## Begin with one documented chain

Abinash Sahoo, Shakti Ranjan Panigrahy and Arpita Mohapatra’s **December 2023 Pahala case study** describes chhena supplied from Niali in Cuttack district, traders carrying it towards Pahala, and sweet making connected with retailing. Its diagram also follows sweets towards commuters, other Odisha markets and West Bengal.

**Chhena producers → traders → Pahala making and retailing → customers**

This simplified reading of the study’s Figure 2 shows roles, not a measured division of earnings. The account interviewed **10 retailers and 200 customers**; fieldwork dates are unstated. It is one case study, not a census of Odisha’s sweet businesses.

## Give each step its own question

| Follow the work | A question for future reporting |
| --- | --- |
| Ingredient supply | Which producer supplied this batch, and what record identifies it? |
| Transport and trading | Who moved it, and which costs belonged to that journey? |
| Making | Who prepared the sweet, and which parts of the work do they want credited? |
| Selling | What was actually sold in an agreed period, and what remained unsold? |

These are reporting prompts. They are not answers collected from a maker, a recipe or instructions for handling food.

The study identifies perishability and packaging among the business questions. Those concerns give a future profile something concrete to investigate. They do not establish a growth forecast or a handling rule for a particular product.

## Keep the shop’s story larger than a revenue headline

The paper’s revenue extrapolation has unresolved quantity and arithmetic conflicts. It is excluded from this article’s account of the market. We cannot turn a shop count and a disputed calculation into measured cluster turnover, or call revenue a maker’s income after costs.

A stronger account would connect a dated batch, completed sales, expenses and actual receipts, with the people involved choosing what they wish to share. Where a record is missing, keep the question open rather than filling it with an attractive estimate.

## Carry the curiosity to another sweet

The existing collection offers other entrances: [Korakhai](../food/korakhai.md), [Dhenkanal Magji](../food/dhenkanal-magji.md) and [Kendrapara Rasabali](../food/kendrapara-rasabali.md). Each has its own source trail and unanswered economic questions. They are not branches of the Pahala study’s supply chain.

For a reader’s notebook, begin with the sweet’s name, the broad place and the maker’s credit where it is shared with permission. Ask one question about the work. A memorable taste can be the start of learning who made it possible.

<details>
<summary>Sources, scope and earlier draft</summary>

[Supply Chain of Pahala Rasagola in Odisha](https://ndpublisher.in/admin/issues/EAv68n5z11.pdf), *Economic Affairs* 68(4), 2305–2308, December 2023, DOI 10.46852/0424-2513.4.2023.37. Original PDF retrieved 11 October 2026. Methods and Figure 2 on printed p.2306, supply roles and constraints on pp.2307–2308 inspected; pp.2306–2307 rendered and visually checked. Figure 2 supplies the chain; Figure 3 instead concerns retailer problems. No diagram, photo, prices or disputed percentages reproduced.

The [sweets-economy record](../references/data/sweets-economy.json) preserves quantity/revenue arithmetic, retailer-percentage denominator and GI-date discrepancies. GI recognition, statewide industry size, current prices, sales growth, foreign exports and food-safety claims are not inferred from this study. Existing other-sweet accounts below remain dated research leads, not newly verified operations or maker interviews.

Creative direction: **Ahimanikya Satapathy**. Developed and reviewed by the current AI assistant. No independent economics or human review, interview, field visit, media-rights clearance or current venue confirmation is claimed. Original draft wording follows intact.

### Earlier draft · 2 October 2026

**A sweet connects more than a shop and a customer.** A published Pahala case study traces chhena from Niali to sweet makers and markets elsewhere in Odisha and West Bengal. It makes dairy supply, preparation and distribution part of the same story. [Study, December 2023, pp.2306–2308](https://ndpublisher.in/admin/issues/EAv68n5z11.pdf).

A useful illustration is a simple chain: **chhena producer → trader → sweet maker and shop → customer**. Show credited people and places once source material and image rights are established.

The research also identifies perishability and packaging as business questions. This is an opportunity to investigate how traditional food reaches wider markets; it is not a measured forecast of growth. The study’s revenue extrapolation is withheld because its quantities and arithmetic conflict.

[Read the evidence and open questions](../economy/rasagola-and-sweets.md) — Connects the story to scoped economic research, preserving sample limits and unresolved market totals.

Editorial draft only. No human review, maker interview, media rights or public release established.

## A rice-based companion story

Korakhai broadens the collection beyond dairy sweets. Its [1999 town-directory entry](https://censusindia.gov.in/nada/index.php/catalog/44136/download/47792/DH_21_2001_KHO.pdf) connects Bhubaneswar’s sweet making with outward trade; [the food entry](../food/korakhai.md) connects it with named confectioners. A possible visual pairs the existing dairy supply chain with this historical rice-based trade record. This is editorial context, not a measured comparison between industries or proof of current export sales.

## People keep the craft moving

The collection now follows a reported Magji family practice in Sadangi and a dated Rasabali market appearance in Bhubaneswar. These suggest portraits of skill and the journey from local preparation to wider selling places. [Magji account](https://interviewtimes.net/dhenkanal-magji-gets-gi-tag/); [Rasabali event reporting](https://www.newindianexpress.com/cities/bhubaneswar/2026/Jan/16/stalls-selling-gi-tagged-products-major-crowd-puller-at-sisir-saras). Use attributed testimony and dated scenes; no sales-growth headline or current maker availability is established.

</details>

title: Taste Odisha: a collection of kitchens
description: A reader story following the cooks, preparation methods and attributed variations behind a first encounter with Odia food.
body:
# Taste Odisha: a collection of kitchens

A food journey can begin with the person who shows you how something is made.

In a 2019 interview by **Mansita Mishra**, chef **Thomas Zacharias** recalls learning about Odia cooking at **Alka Jena’s** home, after an introduction through fellow chef Rachit Kirtiman. He describes a later collaboration with Jena on an Odisha-inspired restaurant menu. A home cook remains visible in the story of how that food travelled.

That is a good place for *Taste Odisha* to begin. Follow a dish back towards the people who prepare it. Let a familiar ingredient surprise you. And leave space for the next cook to do something differently.

## Let the whole meal speak

[Pakhala](../food/pakhala.md) offers one starting point. Odisha Tourism describes a version of rice fermented in water, accompanied by fried vegetables and fish, and associates it with summer. The rice is only part of what you might want to understand: look at what has been placed beside it, and ask how the cook likes to bring the meal together.

In Mishra’s November 2019 menu account, pakhala appears with curd and a ginger-and-mustard tempering. The same menu’s **Habisa Dalma** combines moong with raw banana, arbi and elephant apple. These are dated restaurant descriptions, not instructions for every household or proof of a ritual kitchen’s practice.

When choosing a meal, ask what is being prepared that day. If a cook has time to talk, a small question can open more than a long list: which accompaniment would they miss most if it were absent? What changes when they cook for themselves rather than for guests? Their answer belongs to that person, and might be the part you remember longest.

Our [dalma research](../food/dalma.md) and [preparation collection](../food/preparation-and-variation.md) keep different accounts side by side. You do not have to settle on a single definitive plate before enjoying the conversation.

## A leaf can change what you notice

**Enduri pitha** invites you to look at the wrapping as well as the filling. In **Dr Lipi Das’s** 2015 ICAR compilation, rice-and-black-gram batter and a sweet filling are enclosed in turmeric leaves and steamed. The book also calls it *Haldi Patra Pitha*. Odisha Tourism connects enduri with **Prathamastami**.

If you have an opportunity to try a freshly prepared serving, pause over its shape, surface and aroma. Ask the maker about the leaf and filling they used. Those details give the food a particular identity; “rice cake” alone leaves much unexplained.

The book credits **Ananya Mahila Bikas Samiti** at Sankilo, Cuttack, for information on several Odisha foods, alongside secondary sources. That acknowledgement does not establish that each recipe came from Sankilo.

## Follow the method through the pitha collection

The same book gives several ways to turn rice into something worth stopping for. These are selected preparations in the publication, rather than universal recipes or an exhaustive pitha list.

| Preparation | What to look for in this source’s version |
| --- | --- |
| [Chakuli](../food/chakuli.md) | Batter spread and cooked on a pan; the book includes an onion-and-herb version. |
| [Enduri](../food/enduri-pitha.md) | Filled batter folded inside turmeric leaves, then steamed. |
| [Manda](../food/manda-pitha.md) | Filled rice dough shaped and steamed. |
| [Kakara](../food/kakara-pitha.md) | A rice-and-wheat-flour casing with sweet coconut filling, fried. |

Compare two preparations if they are available. What changes when a batter is spread rather than enclosed? What does a filling add? You can build a tasting around those questions without trying to finish an entire culinary checklist.

Names alone do not settle every method. Odisha Tourism calls its *sijha manda* boiled; the ICAR version above is steamed. Our research retains that distinction for local clarification. Ask the cook what they call their preparation and how they make it. A useful food notebook has room for more than one answer.

## Leave room for a changing sweet

[Chhena poda](../food/chhena-poda.md) brings the journey to a baked sweet. Odisha Tourism describes sweetened fresh-curd cheese baked under sal leaves in an earthen oven. That is one documented preparation to read alongside the slice you encounter.

In a contribution published on 29 July 2021, **Chef Michael** offers a chocolate adaptation using chhena or paneer. It is explicitly his contemporary recipe. You can be curious about an adaptation while still wanting to understand the preparation that inspired it.

Ask what the maker has kept, what they have changed, and why. Compare the surface with the centre; give your own impressions words before borrowing someone else’s verdict. This is an invitation to taste attentively, not a ranking of cooks or a verdict on which version alone belongs to Odisha.

## Bring an appetite—and a little time

For a first food outing, choose a manageable focus: one meal, two pitha preparations, or a sweet and the story of its maker. Check that the place currently serves what you want before travelling specifically for it. Historical articles and recipe pages do not establish today’s menu, hours or availability.

Ask about the ingredients in the actual serving if you have dietary needs; a dish name is not enough. If you would like a photograph, a recording or a recipe to share, ask permission and keep the cook’s credit attached. A private home mentioned in a published interview is not an open visitor venue.

Keep three things from the experience: the name of the preparation, who made or explained it, and one detail you would tell a friend. The next kitchen may give you another version. That is a reason to keep exploring.

## Sources and preparation notes

- [Mansita Mishra, interview with Thomas Zacharias, Odisha Tourism, 27 November 2019](https://apps.odishatourism.gov.in/blog-detail/chef-tzac-odia-cuisine-is-an-evolved-cuisine): collaboration answer and menu sections. Re-inspected 10 October 2026. Used for named credit and dated preparations; no claim of current affiliation, menu availability or access to Jena’s home.
- [The Taste of Odisha](https://apps.odishatourism.gov.in/the-taste-of-odisha): Pakhala, Sijha Manda, Enduri and Chennapoda entries, re-inspected 10 October 2026. Institutional descriptions; health assertions, universal household claims and unsupported origin claims excluded.
- [Dr Lipi Das, *Traditional Rice Foods: The Rich Heritage of India*, ICAR-CRRI, 2015](https://icar-crri.in/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/final_book_ldas.pdf): preface PDF p.6; printed pp.12,19,21,24 / PDF pp.23,30,32,35. Original PDF recovered and passages inspected, with the enduri page also checked visually. This compilation documents versions; we have not recipe-tested them. The 2023 URL folder is not the book’s publication year.
- [Chef Michael, “CHHENAPODA”, Odisha Tourism, 29 July 2021](https://apps.odishatourism.gov.in/blog-detail/chhenapoda): contemporary chocolate recipe, re-inspected 10 October 2026. Historical invention and sales claims are not adopted. The tourism overview and hosted contributions share a platform, although the bylined accounts have distinct authors.

## Campaign and production record

This expands the earlier campaign concept in Git revision `298d342c`; its line remains **“One state. So many ways to welcome you.”** The article introduces selected examples, not every community’s cuisine. Reader response has not been measured, and no visit, tasting, interview or contributor relationship is claimed.

Retain the earlier formats: a named dish poster with one grounded sensory line; a short feature with one maker, preparation, variation and occasion; and a video moving from serving to the maker’s voice, process and finished plate. A national-audience version can test “your next food journey”; an international version should retain local names with plain-language explanations.

Original photographs should make the method legible: a leaf being folded, batter on a pan, a filled preparation cut open, and the whole serving. Obtain contributor consent and image rights, verify names and ingredients with the featured cook, and check current business details before publication. These are production proposals, not commissioned assets. The earlier idea of a Founder AI-clone introduction remains unproduced and depends on a separately selected service and asset.

This is a KB draft with same-assistant review. Local/Odia review, recipe testing and an illustrated website edition remain separate work. The existing food research and its unresolved variations remain authoritative; this story does not close those follow-ups.

title: Utkal: a trading culture, building its next global chapter
description: Utkal: a trading culture, building its next global chapter — evidence, scope and reuse.
body:
# Utkal: a trading culture, building its next global chapter

## Production brief · a shore, a memory, a question

**Deliverable now:** a proposed 90-second editorial film script and scene plan. No film, recording session, permission, commissioned participant or external campaign has been produced or activated. This brief develops the earlier concept preserved below. It invites people to read and ask questions; it does not promote a held shop, offer investment advice or solicit business on another organisation’s behalf.

The audience is someone who knows Odisha through a festival, a journey or a family memory and wants to understand its wider connections. Begin with a small, tangible thing, move through one dated institutional event, then leave the viewer curious about the people and work behind trade. The connection between remembrance and contemporary work is editorial framing, not evidence of an uninterrupted historical business lineage.

### Six scenes and original narration

Timing is a planning allocation, not a measured voice performance. Allow quiet pauses and adjust after a read-through. All words below are original proposed narration; none is a quotation, a historical testimony or a participant’s account.

| Time | Proposed voice | Image and evidence requirement | Fallback if material is unavailable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0–12s | “A small boat can hold a large question. Who left this shore? What did they carry? What stayed in the memory of those who waited?” | Close view of a permitted, identified ritual boat or museum model. Identify which it is. Do not present a model as an ancient vessel or stage a family ritual as observed documentary. | Simple boat outline on paper, explicitly treated as illustration; no claim that it depicts an actual artefact. |
| 12–27s | “In November 2023, Paradip Port Authority organised Boita Bandana. Here, a contemporary institution took part in remembering maritime exchange.” | Use the [dated institutional record](../trade/paradip-bridge.md). Event images need separate reuse clearance and a visible date. A public release is evidence of the event, not an automatic footage licence. | Date card: “Paradip · 27 November 2023”; source in end notes. No simulated footage of the President or ceremony. |
| 27–42s | “Memory gives us an opening. To understand trade today, look at what is made, what is moved, and what the records actually measure.” | Verified, dated present-day work imagery only if location, access and rights are documented. Port throughput, state merchandise exports and company sales are different scopes. Do not use a port shot to prove the origin of a particular cargo. | Three labelled editorial cards: “Making · Moving · Measuring”, with no unsupported numbers or cargo routes. |
| 42–60s | “Behind a product is work. A fuller story would begin with one person’s part in it: their skill, their choices, and the account they are willing to share.” | Future willing participant and actual role needed. Record permission for identity, voice and work separately. Show the person’s contribution without inventing a customer, destination or earnings claim. | A still-life of permitted tools with accurate context, or a quiet question card. Do not generate a fictional named maker or synthetic testimony. |
| 60–78s | “One company’s exports are not the whole state. A busy port is not a household’s income. A good story keeps its scale—and leaves room for what we do not yet know.” | Link the [ferrochrome case](odisha-ferrochrome-markets.md) and [supplier case](minerals-and-local-suppliers.md) as reading, not visuals that assert a direct shared supply chain. No automatic conversion between tonnes, turnover and livelihoods. | Text-led scene with readable measure labels; keep it a question about evidence rather than a numerical claim. |
| 78–90s | “Come closer. Read a story. Bring a question. The next chapter begins with what we can understand, and what we choose to build together.” | End on “Utkal Project” and a reading link to the [maritime story](narratives/maritime-memory.json). Invitation is editorial; no partnership, volunteer appointment or operating business implied. | Static end card and descriptive link text. |

### A coherent visual and sound language

Use [current brand direction](../../reference/brand-direction-02.md): Nila Sagara for main titles, Mankada Pathara for a word of emphasis, warm paper for quieter reading moments, and restrained Sukha Ghasi accents. The older palette sentence in the preserved concept is historical and superseded for this production brief. Keep English and Odia marks separate; an Odia narration or subtitle edition requires an actual language review before release.

Let the boat, a dated card, working material and a final reading invitation form the visual progression. Keep cuts unhurried. Distinguish an archival event from contemporary scenes with visible dates rather than allowing the edit to imply they happened together. If illustrative material is used, identify its role in context and credits; realism must not manufacture documentary evidence.

Use recorded ambient sound only with a known source and rights. Music must have a documented reusable licence, composition permission or verified public-domain basis for the relevant recording. A traditional melody does not automatically free a modern recording. Keep music below narration; retain meaningful quiet. No paid music/video service is authorized by this brief.

### Handoff and acceptance before a film release

Build one media manifest with scene ID, file, creator, source URL or capture record, capture/event date, place, depicted subject, licence/permission scope, credit, edits and evidence limitations. Unavailable is a real status. Keep source claims separate from media rights; a beautiful picture cannot clear either by itself.

Before rendering a release candidate, the editor should verify each used asset and factual caption, record the actual voice performer and read-through duration, and resolve or replace every blocked scene. Do not book people, contact institutions or obtain access as part of this desk brief. New commitments require their own authorized scope.

A later playable candidate needs accurate captions, an accessible transcript, descriptive player labelling, pause/mute controls and no automatic sound. Important dates and measure scopes must be readable on mobile, with end credits long enough to read or available in a persistent linked panel. Check the final cut muted, with sound and on a small screen; record actual outcomes. The 90-second plan is not a test result or proof of completed video.

**Evidence checkpoint:** the President’s Secretariat/PIB [27 November 2023 release](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=1980175) was re-read on 11 October 2026 for the organiser and dated event only. Other linked research is reused with its saved scope and limitations; this brief makes no fresh numerical trade claim or new historical finding. Same-assistant review is not independent human, language, participant or film review.

<details>
<summary>Preserved earlier campaign concept</summary>

## Positioning

**Utkal · Odisha**

**A trading culture. A new global chapter.**

The commercial proposition is that Odisha already has modern trade activity worth showing, and a distinctive way to introduce it. Heritage supplies the opening; present evidence supplies the business case.

## Story sequence

Open with [Boita Bandana](../culture/boita-bandana.md), then show the [Paradip institutional connection](../trade/paradip-bridge.md). Move to the port’s measured activity and the state’s merchandise-export comparison. End with a named maker or business, researched separately, and a useful next action.

The question “If we could do it then, why can’t we do it now?” becomes: **“We are trading today. What can we build next?”** This invites ambition without pretending that an ancient achievement forecasts modern performance.

## Three campaign directions

- **Trade has a place in our culture.** A ritual-led film connected to an actual institution and its work.
- **Odisha is already connected.** A contemporary trade feature with destinations, products and counterparties as the evidence grows.
- **The next voyage begins with what we make.** A maker or exporter portrait leading to an attributable purchase or business enquiry.

## Copy ready for development

“Every voyage begins with the courage to look beyond the shore. In Odisha, the memory of the maritime trader is still celebrated. Today, a new chapter is being written by the people who make, move and trade. Meet the Odisha building its place in the world.”

This is campaign copy. Support accompanying factual captions through the [headline bank](../trade/headline-bank.md). The line does not assert that every modern enterprise descends from ancient traders.

## Creative treatment

Use the project’s deep red, ivory and ochre palette. Pair miniature boats with contemporary activity through an editorial transition, not a simulated historical reconstruction presented as documentary footage. Mark illustrative animation as illustration. Include local voices and credited work.

## Claim discipline

Choose strong facts and clear comparisons. Do not knowingly create a false impression by dropping the unit, hiding a crucial denominator, converting an interpretation into certainty, or making a proposed project look operational. That preserves the campaign’s ability to stand up to scrutiny.

</details>

title: Forest products, local enterprise: a documented Odisha strength
description: Named historical clusters connect product processing to the question of who receives the value.

sources.title: Lok Sabha question 1179: economic development of tribal communities
Benefiting the tribal livelihoods of Odisha through the Van Dhan Yojana

publication_scope: Repository article draft; not a website release
body:
# Forest products, local enterprise: a documented Odisha strength

**Look beyond the finished product. Ask about the work between gathering and selling.**

A leaf plate is a useful starting point. It invites us to notice a material, a way of making and the people whose work carries it towards a customer. Odisha’s existing enterprise records offer names to begin with—and questions that a sales total alone cannot answer.

## Follow a product towards its makers

A **4 May 2021 Ministry of Tribal Affairs account** describes planned processing in named Van Dhan clusters. The table below follows that historical account; it is not a directory of businesses operating today.

| Historical lead | Place in the account | Planned product work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Luguburu, Maa Dharithri and Bhimakund, collectively | Mayurbhanj | Sal-leaf plates and cups, kusum oil and processed wild honey |
| Anchalika Khandadhar | Keonjhar | Mango preparations, turmeric powder and mustard oil |
| Ban Durga | District not stated in the relevant paragraph | Deseeded tamarind, tamarind cake, sal shampoo and packed char seeds |

Keep the three Mayurbhanj names together: the source does not assign every product to each cluster. Its plans and general early-production description do not establish which group subsequently sold what.

Still, the leads give us a way to look more closely. Processing, packaging and finding a buyer are different steps. For a future profile, follow one product through those steps with the people willing to explain their work. Ask which tasks they undertake and what they want a reader to understand. No such interview is claimed here.

## Put the sales figure in its own frame

An **11 December 2023 parliamentary reply** reports **₹1,072.01 lakh**, or **₹10.7201 crore**, in cumulative Odisha Van Dhan sales. Odisha had the highest reported amount among that annexure’s 28 state/UT rows: about **26.1%** of its ₹4,102.95 lakh total.

This is historical programme reporting, covering both minor forest produce and non-MFP activities. It is not annual turnover, Odisha’s whole forest economy or a present-day ranking. The reply does not specify a precise common sales cutoff.

Nor can the statewide sum be distributed across the named clusters above. Their individual sales and collector payments require separate evidence. A sanctioned centre is not proof of an operating shop, and a beneficiary count is not an income statement.

## What would make the next account stronger?

Start with one product, a defined period and an agreed account of the work. Match completed sales with processing costs and payments actually received by collectors or producers. Keep these different measures beside one another rather than letting a large headline stand in for all of them.

For readers, the invitation can be smaller: ask who made a product and how its material was processed. Record or publish someone’s explanation only with their permission and agreed credit. These historical cluster names confer no access to a community or workshop, and this page makes no purchase or visit promise.

Continue through the [forest-product economy research](../economy/forest-products.md), or read how [worker support](forest-worker-support.md) differs from trade earnings. The story worth pursuing is what the people doing the work choose to share, supported by records that show where the value went.

<details>
<summary>Sources, calculations and earlier draft</summary>

[Ministry of Tribal Affairs / PIB, 4 May 2021](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=1715921), named-cluster paragraphs, re-read 11 October 2026. Product lists retain their collective and planned scope; district, current ownership and current operation are not inferred. General positive-impact language is not adopted as measured household evidence.

[Lok Sabha question 1179, answer 11 December 2023](https://sansad.in/getFile/loksabhaquestions/annex/1714/AU1179.pdf?source=pqals), PDF pp.1 and3. Original reply retrieved and the annexure rendered/visually checked 11 October 2026. ₹1,072.01 lakh ÷100 = ₹10.7201 crore; 1,072.01 ÷4,102.95 ×100 = about26.1%. The table’s reported total is the denominator; its scope is cumulative programme reporting. The [statistics page](../statistics/forest-products.md) preserves earlier vintages and other categories separately.

Creative direction: **Ahimanikya Satapathy**. Developed and reviewed by the current AI assistant. No independent economics or human review, interviews, field visits, community relationships or current service confirmation is claimed. Earlier wording and canonical research remain preserved.

### Earlier draft · 2 October 2026

**₹10.72 crore in reported Van Dhan sales placed Odisha highest in a December 2023 parliamentary table.** The underlying figure is ₹1,072.01 lakh, covering cumulative programme reporting rather than one year's turnover. [Reply, annexure p.3](https://sansad.in/getFile/loksabhaquestions/annex/1714/AU1179.pdf?source=pqals).

Odisha accounted for about **26.1%** of the published all-India programme total. This includes both forest and non-forest products; it is not a measure of the entire forest economy, exports or collector income.

One way to tell the human story is to follow the work: a leaf becomes a plate, honey is processed, and tamarind is deseeded. A [2021 ministry account](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=1715921) names community clusters pursuing these activities. Their individual sales and current operations remain research questions.

Suggested campaign direction: **“The value of a forest also lives in the work of its people.”** This is editorial wording, not a measured income-impact claim. Keep the December 2023 date visible in any card or poster; this evidence does not support a present-day ranking.

[Related reading](../statistics/forest-products.md) — Explains the programme denominator and separates turnover from collector receipts.

[Related reading](../economy/forest-products.md) — Connects named historical enterprises to product research without claiming current operation.
